item.title: GDPR and Keycloak: erasure, retention, and residency
item.description: Which GDPR obligations Keycloak can satisfy, which it silently leaves to you, and which are decided by where you run it. Every claim tested on Keycloak 26.8.2.
item.content:encoded:
Keycloak gives you a working mechanism for roughly half of what the GDPR asks of an identity provider, no mechanism at all for the other half, and — the part that costs people — one mechanism that looks like it worked and did not. It has no concept of a data subject request, no data export for one person, no retention default other than forever, and no setting anywhere called residency. What it does have is a complete admin API over every record it keeps, which is enough to build the rest if you know which four gaps to fill. This post maps each obligation to the mechanism that actually serves it, tested against Keycloak 26.8.2 on 2026-11-09, including the moment where a user erases their own account and Keycloak writes a fresh record of their username and IP address on the way out.

This is an engineering read of the regulation, not legal advice. Where a thing is a judgement call for your DPO rather than a setting, it says so.

What the official documentation covers​

One page. The Server Administration Guide has a section called Personal data collected by Keycloak, and it is three bullets long: basic profile data, the same for social logins, and "device information collected for audit and security purposes, such as the IP address, operating system name, and the browser name." Then three guidelines about customisation, credentials being hashed, and authorization services holding object ownership.

That is accurate and it is the whole of it. There is no official guidance on erasure, on retention, on building a subject access package, or on where any of it is stored. Everything below is the part the guide skips.

The mapping, obligation by obligation​

ObligationKeycloak mechanismWhat you still have to supply
Art. 15 accessGET /users/{id}, /credentials, /sessions, /consents, /events?user=The assembly, the format, and the one-month clock
Art. 16 rectificationAdmin API and Account ConsoleNothing — this one is complete
Art. 17 erasureDELETE /users/{id}; self-service Delete Account actionEvent store, admin-event representations, backups, logs
Art. 18 restrictionenabled: false — the closest thing there isEverything else; see below
Art. 20 portabilityPer-user JSON from the admin API; kc.sh export for the realmA machine-readable format a human asked for
Art. 21 / 7(3) objection and withdrawalDELETE /users/{id}/consents/{clientId}Knowing that this, not logout, is the one that works
Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitationeventsExpiration, adminEventsExpiration, session timeouts, workflowsYour log pipeline, which Keycloak does not manage
Art. 25 data protection by designUnmanaged attributes are off by defaultWatching what happens when you turn them on
Art. 30 records of processingThe admin API is the inventoryThe document
Art. 32 securityArgon2id by default, brute-force detection, TLSOperations
Art. 33 breach notificationAdmin events plus an event listenerThe 72-hour chain and someone to run it
Chapter V transfersNothing. Keycloak has no region, no residency flagWhere you run it, and who can log in to administer it

Two rows in that table are not what most teams assume, and one row is empty. Those three are the rest of this post.

Art. 15: there is no export button, so here is the package​

Nothing in Keycloak assembles "everything you hold about me". Five endpoints hold the parts, and in 26.8.2 they return this:

# profile, including any custom attributes
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" \
  "$KC/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$UID"

# credential metadata — note what this does and does not contain
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" \
  "$KC/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$UID/credentials"
[
  {
    "id": "120dd02a-953b-412f-bdd4-6b66688ee666",
    "type": "password",
    "createdDate": 1794214768785,
    "credentialData": "{\"hashIterations\":5,\"algorithm\":\"argon2\",\"additionalParameters\":{\"hashLength\":[\"32\"],\"memory\":[\"7168\"],\"type\":[\"id\"],\"version\":[\"1.3\"],\"parallelism\":[\"1\"]}}"
  }
]

The credentials endpoint returns metadata and no secretData: the algorithm, the parameters and the creation date, never the hash or the salt. That is the right answer for a subject access request — the person is entitled to know that you hold a password credential and how it is protected, not to receive the material that authenticates them. It is also a small piece of free evidence for an Art. 32 answer, since it shows what your realm is actually hashing with rather than what you believe it is.

Then sessions, consents, and the event rows:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" "$KC/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$UID/sessions"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" "$KC/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$UID/consents"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" "$KC/admin/realms/$REALM/events?user=$UID"

Sessions carry the IP address. Events carry the IP address, the username, the client, and in details a set of per-event fields that varies by type. Both are personal data about an identified person and both belong in the package.

The user-facing half is the Account REST API, which the Account Console runs on and which you can call directly with the user's own token:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $UAT" -H "Accept: application/json" \
  "$KC/realms/$REALM/account/sessions/devices"
[{"os":"Other","device":"Other","lastAccess":1794214885,"current":true,
  "sessions":[{"id":"6R6fqTy-CYlfsRSYLUxpYunj","ipAddress":"172.17.0.1",
  "started":1794214885,"expires":1794250885,"browser":"curl/8.18.0"}]}]

Useful to know when a DPO asks whether the person can see this themselves: for profile, devices, linked accounts and credential metadata, yes. For the event store, no — there is no self-service view of it, so that part of an access request lands on you.

Art. 17: the deletion writes a new record about the person​

The documentation for the self-service Delete Account action says: "This action is irreversible. All your data in Keycloak will be removed."

We ran it. A realm with events enabled, a user called bruno, the delete_account required action enabled and the delete-account role assigned; then the real browser flow, kc_action=delete_account, login, confirm. The account goes:

confirm:200
GET /admin/realms/gdpr/users/62277568-... -> 404 {"error":"User not found"}

And the event store gains a row:

{"type": "DELETE_ACCOUNT",
 "userId": "62277568-bf43-4f6f-bb20-aa35b2add13c",
 "ipAddress": "172.17.0.1",
 "details": {"username": "bruno", "custom_required_action": "delete_account", ...}}

The act of erasure is itself logged as an event containing the erased person's username, their internal id and the IP address they did it from — and with no expiration set, which is the default, that row has no end date. The same is true of the admin API route: after DELETE /users/{id} returns 204 and the user returns 404, GET /events?user={id} still returns their logins with username and IP, and a stored admin-event representation still carries their email address and phone number as plain JSON.

None of that makes the delete wrong. Audit records of a deletion have a defensible basis, and you may well need them. It makes "all your data will be removed" wrong, which matters, because that sentence is what a team quotes to its DPO. Erasure on Keycloak is a delete plus a decision about the event store, and the inventory of exactly what remains and where is in what personal data Keycloak stores and how to erase it.

Art. 18 and 7(3): disable is not restriction, and logout is not withdrawal​

Setting enabled: false is the only lever that resembles restriction of processing. Here is precisely what it reaches, on 26.8.2:

After PUT {"enabled": false}Result
New loginsRefused
Refresh tokeninvalid_grant — "User disabled"
Token introspection at the resource server{"active": false} immediately
/userinfo with the existing access token401
The existing access token, validated locally against the realm JWKSStill passes, for the rest of its lifetime
The user's session row, with its IP addressStill there

The fifth row is the one to design around. An access token that was minted before you disabled the account still verifies against the realm's public key, still contains preferred_username and email, and any resource server doing offline JWT validation — which is the recommended pattern for most APIs — will keep accepting it until exp. On a stock realm that is 300 seconds:

iat 1794214821 exp 1794215121 lifetime_s 300

Five minutes is fine for an offboarding. It is not fine as an answer to "processing has been restricted as of now", and it is not fine if someone has raised accessTokenLifespan to an hour to cut traffic. If you need processing to stop at a defined instant, the resource server has to introspect, or you have to accept the token lifespan as your true response time and write that number down.

Withdrawal of consent has the same shape of trap, in the other direction. An admin logout does not do it:

curl -X POST .../users/$UID/logout      # 204
curl -d "grant_type=refresh_token" -d "refresh_token=$OFFLINE_RT" .../token
# -> {"access_token": "...", "expires_in": 300, ...}

A 204, and the offline refresh token still mints access tokens. Offline tokens survive logout by design — that is what offline access is — and on a stock realm they live for 30 days (refresh_expires_in: 2592000). The thing that actually ends them is revoking the grant:

curl -X DELETE .../users/$UID/consents/app       # 204
curl -d "grant_type=refresh_token" -d "refresh_token=$OFFLINE_RT" .../token
# -> {"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"Offline user session not found"}

So when someone withdraws consent or asks you to stop, DELETE /users/{id}/consents/{clientId} is the call. POST /logout reports success and leaves a 30-day credential in the hands of the application you were asked to cut off. The consents endpoint is also how you find them: an offline token shows up there as an additionalGrants entry labelled Offline Token, which is the only place the admin API names it in plain language.

Art. 5(1)(e): four retention clocks, three of them unset​

Storage limitation is not one setting. For an identity provider it is four, and Keycloak ships three of them switched off.

  1. Events. Off by default; once on, kept forever unless you set an expiration, and the two expirations live in two different places with two different APIs. The mechanics, the units, and what the purge actually does are in Keycloak event retention: expiration settings for GDPR.

  2. Sessions and offline sessions. These do have defaults — 10 hours for an SSO session, 30 days for an offline one — which is to say they have defaults you chose by not changing them. An offline session is a 30-day record of a person's device and IP.

  3. The accounts themselves. A dormant account is retained personal data, and nothing deletes one. Keycloak now ships workflows for exactly this — notify, then disable, then delete on a schedule — and on 26.8.2 the WORKFLOWS feature is enabled by default, which we confirmed against the server's own feature list. The trap is that the obvious rule also deletes service accounts and takes their clients down with them. The tested version is in automating offboarding and deprovisioning.

  4. The log stream, which nobody counts. The default event listener is jboss-logging, so error events go to stdout at WARN:

    WARN [org.keycloak.events] type="LOGIN_ERROR", realmName="gdpr",
    clientId="app", userId="7f9703d0-...", ipAddress="172.17.0.1",
    error="invalid_user_credentials", username="erika"

    No successful login appeared in the container log at the default level; every failure did. Username and IP, leaving the database entirely, into a pipeline with its own retention, its own access control and frequently its own region. Keycloak's retention settings do not reach one line of it.

Art. 25: the silent 204​

Try to store an attribute Keycloak does not know about:

curl -X PUT -d '{"username":"erika", ..., "attributes":{"phoneNumber":["+49 30 1234567"]}}' \
  .../users/$UID
# 204
curl .../users/$UID | jq .attributes
# -> absent

The write is accepted, the attribute is dropped, and nothing tells you. Unmanaged attributes are Disabled by default in Keycloak 26, which is a genuinely good default — declared attributes only, data minimisation enforced by the schema. Set unmanagedAttributePolicy: ENABLED on /users/profile and the identical request stores the phone number.

Both states have a consequence worth knowing before an audit. Left at the default, an integration that thinks it is writing a national ID or a birthday is writing nothing, and your record of processing says you hold a field you do not. Switched on — commonly during a migration, and then left on — every attribute anything writes becomes stored personal data that no schema declares and no DPO has seen. Declare the attributes you need in the user profile and turn the policy back off when the migration ends.

Chapter V: residency is not a Keycloak setting​

There is no region field. Keycloak stores what you point it at, so the question "where does our identity data live" has five answers and none of them is in the realm configuration:

Where identity data landsWhat decides its location
The databaseYour --db-url
Sessions and cacheYour Infinispan topology, and whether it spans sites
The event storeThe same database, unless an event listener ships events elsewhere
BackupsYour backup policy and the region you replicate to
Logs and metricsYour log pipeline, which is usually the least EU thing you own

And a sixth that is not storage at all: who can authenticate to the admin console, and from where. Remote administrative access to EU-hosted data from outside the EU is a restricted transfer under Chapter V even when no byte is copied out, which is the argument that catches vendors whose data map is clean and whose on-call rota is not. The network layer of that is configurable; the organisational layer is a staffing decision.

If you are working through this as a buyer rather than an operator, the three companion pieces are data residency vs data sovereignty for your identity provider, the DPO's checklist for a SaaS authentication vendor, and what a US parent actually means under the CLOUD Act.

Where we stand​

On our EU data residency clusters: the Keycloak database, sessions, the event store and the realm signing keys are in Frankfurt (eu-central-1), backups are in Ireland (eu-west-1), and identity data is never replicated outside the EU. Backups are retained for 30 days, which is also the answer to "when is an erasure complete in your backups" — the live delete is immediate, the backup copies age out within the window, and a restore does not resurrect an erased record. The detail is in backups and data retention.

The unflattering half, in the same place: our control plane runs in the United States, our engineering team is distributed, and administrative access to an EU cluster can therefore come from outside the EU. That is a restricted transfer and we disclose it rather than describing EU-only administration we do not operate by default. You contract with Phase Two UK, Ltd (company number 16815578, registered in England and Wales); Phase Two, Inc. in Seattle is the parent. EU→UK transfers run on the European Commission's renewed adequacy decision of 2025-12-19, which runs to 2031-12-27. We are not certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework and do not rely on it for EU customer data. Dashboard metadata, support tickets and billing are in the US, so do not put end-user personal data in a support ticket. We have received zero government or law-enforcement requests to date. The regulatory facts in this paragraph were re-checked on 2026-11-09. Our data processing agreement carries Art. 28(3) terms with contractual incident notification in 48–72 hours, which is short enough to feed your own Art. 33 clock. Support is in English only.

What we could not make work​

Three honest gaps, because they will come up in your own review:

  • There is no per-user export in the admin API. POST /partial-export has a users key, which is the trap: on a realm with one human user and one service account it returned a single entry, and that entry was the service account. Real users come out of kc.sh export or out of iterating /users yourself. The exit path for a whole realm, with what it loses, is in exporting a realm for portability.
  • Erasure cannot reach a token already issued. Nothing in Keycloak invalidates a JWT that a resource server validates offline. Your true response time for "stop processing now" is your access token lifespan, whatever you set it to.
  • We did not test SQL-level residue beyond what the admin API exposes. The API view and the table view agreed everywhere we checked them, but the authoritative inventory is the database one.

The next step, if you are standing a realm up for a European deployment: enable events, set both expirations on day one rather than after the first audit, declare your attributes in the user profile and leave unmanaged attributes disabled, and decide — before anyone asks — whether your answer to "processing has stopped" is introspection or a token lifespan.

If you would rather the storage, backup and key-residency half of that list were somebody else's problem, that is what EU data residency on our managed clusters is for, and our data processing agreement is available to your DPO without an NDA.

item.title: Native login for Keycloak: sign users in with your app's own screens on iOS and Android
item.description: Phase Two's open native authentication for Keycloak lets iOS and Android apps sign users in with native screens instead of a browser. Passwords, passkeys, TOTP, one-time codes, push approvals and step-up run in the app, on top of Keycloak's own authentication flows.
item.content:encoded:
Today we're opening up native authentication for Keycloak: a set of Keycloak extensions and iOS and Android SDKs that let a mobile app sign users in with its own screens instead of a browser. Passwords, passkeys, TOTP, email and SMS codes, recovery codes, push approvals with number matching, step-up and required actions all run natively, while Keycloak still decides what the user has to do. The SDKs are Apache 2.0, and the code is on GitHub.

Why we built it​

The standard way to add Keycloak login to a mobile app is the system browser: the app opens Keycloak's login page in an in-app browser sheet, the user signs in, and the browser hands an authorization code back to the app. It's secure and it's what we've recommended for years, in our own native apps guide too. It also has costs that product teams keep raising with us. The iOS "wants to use … to sign in" prompt appears before the user sees anything. The login page is a web page inside a native app, themed to look native but never quite matching. And every factor the flow asks for is a web page, so passkeys, push approvals and biometrics don't feel like part of the app.

The alternative most teams reach for is worse: the password grant, where the app posts a username and password straight to the token endpoint. It only handles passwords, it skips the authentication flow entirely, so MFA, required actions and brute-force rules configured in Keycloak don't apply, and OAuth 2.1 drops it.

The IETF has been working on a better answer, OAuth 2.0 for First-Party Applications (FiPA): the app talks to an authorization challenge endpoint, the server answers with what it needs next, and the app collects it natively until the server issues an authorization code. We built that for Keycloak, and SDKs that turn it into native screens.

How it works​

The Keycloak extensions add a challenge endpoint to each realm. A login starts with a request from the app, and Keycloak runs the client's normal authentication flow. Instead of rendering a login page, each step comes back as a structured JSON challenge:

{
  "error": "insufficient_authorization",
  "auth_session": "<opaque>",
  "challenges": [
    { "type": "username", "id": "<execution>", "label": "Username", "required": true }
  ]
}

The SDK shows the matching screen, sends the answer back, and repeats until Keycloak returns an authorization code, which the SDK exchanges for tokens with PKCE. Because Keycloak is still running the flow, everything you configure there applies: conditional second factors, brute-force protection, required actions, levels of authentication for step-up. You change the login in the admin console, not in the app.

Anything the native flow can't handle falls back to the system browser for that login, so a social login button or a custom authenticator without a native version still works.

What runs natively​

  • Passwords and saved passwords. Both SDKs work with the platform password managers: AutoFill on iOS and Credential Manager on Android, including saving a new password after sign-in.
  • Passkeys. Sign in with a passkey using the platform APIs, enroll one right after a password login, or register one later from inside the app.
  • Second factors. TOTP, email and SMS one-time codes, and recovery codes, each as a native screen with the countdowns and "try another way" choices you'd expect.
  • Push approvals. Users enroll their phone from the app and approve sign-ins with number matching, through APNs on iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging on Android. Push builds on ba-itsys' open-source Keycloak push MFA extension.
  • Step-up. An app can ask for a higher level of authentication for a sensitive action, such as a transfer, and the user only answers the extra factor.
  • Required actions. Updating a password, verifying an email with a code, accepting terms and registering a passkey happen in the app instead of bouncing to the browser.

Sessions and tokens can be bound to a key on the device with DPoP, so a token copied off the device can't be used without that key. The SDKs keep tokens in the Keychain on iOS and the Android Keystore on Android.

SDKs with default screens you can replace​

Each SDK has a core layer and a UI layer. The core handles the protocol: the challenge loop, PKCE, DPoP, tokens, refresh and logout, credential storage, and push. The UI layer adds default screens for every challenge type, in SwiftUI on iOS and Jetpack Compose on Android, so a working login is a few lines of code. Any screen can be replaced with your own design, one challenge type at a time, and you can skip the UI layer entirely and build every screen yourself.

The repository also has demo apps for both platforms and a Docker Compose setup with a preconfigured realm, so you can try every flow on your laptop.

Tested against Keycloak itself​

Every exchange between the SDKs and Keycloak is recorded by the extensions' integration tests, which run against real Keycloak 26.4, 26.6 and 26.8 servers. Both SDKs replay those recordings in their own test suites, so a change on the server that would break a client fails the build before it ships. The protocol is written up in the repository for anyone building a client on another platform.

What stays in the browser​

Some flows belong on Keycloak's own pages, so they stay in the browser: new-user registration, forgotten-password recovery, TOTP enrollment, and social and enterprise identity-provider login.

Try it​

The native-apps repository has the extensions, both SDKs, the demo apps and the developer documentation. The project is below 1.0, so the protocol and APIs may still change between releases. The SDKs and demo setup are Apache 2.0, and the Keycloak extensions are under the Elastic License 2.0, like our other extensions. If you'd like native login on a Phase Two hosted Keycloak, or help bringing it into your app, get in touch.

item.title: Login Tracer: debug SAML and OIDC logins in Chrome DevTools
item.description: Login Tracer by Phase Two is a free Chrome DevTools extension that decodes SAML and OIDC/OAuth logins, verifies signatures offline, flags misconfigurations, and exports a redacted trace. No permissions, no network requests.
item.content:encoded:
Today we're releasing Login Tracer by Phase Two, a free Chrome DevTools extension for debugging SAML and OpenID Connect / OAuth logins. Open DevTools, select the Login Tracer panel, and log in: every SSO request in the tab is decoded, grouped into a login flow, and checked for common misconfigurations, with explanations of the Keycloak setting most likely behind each problem. It requests no permissions and makes no network requests.

Why we built it​

Most of the SSO problems we help with come down to one question: what did the browser actually send, and what came back? Answering it usually means opening the Network panel, finding the right redirect among dozens of requests, copying a SAMLResponse or a token, and pasting it into a decoder website. That last step is the uncomfortable one. A SAML assertion or an access token is a live credential, and pasting it into a third-party site means trusting that site with it.

Browser extensions that trace logins already exist, and several decode SAML and OIDC well. What we kept missing was the next step: checking that a signature actually verifies against the identity provider's keys, explaining which setting most likely caused the failure, and following a brokered login from the app to Keycloak to an upstream identity provider and back as one flow. Some of them also ask to read and change data on every website you visit, all the time, not just while you are debugging.

We wanted a tool that shows the whole login, SAML and OIDC alike, and that cannot leak what it sees. We already had the decoding logic from our in-browser SAML Decoder and JWT Decoder, so we built Login Tracer on top of it as a DevTools panel.

What it shows​

Login flows. Requests are grouped into flows by state, nonce, authorization code, SAML request ID and InResponseTo, and RelayState. A brokered login that goes from your app to Keycloak, on to an external identity provider, and back shows up as one flow with both legs, and each flow gets a timeline across hosts.

SAML. AuthnRequest, Response, LogoutRequest, and LogoutResponse over the HTTP-Redirect and HTTP-POST bindings, plus WS-Federation sign-in. You get the pretty-printed XML and a summary of the issuer, destination, ACS URL, audience, NameID, conditions, attributes, signatures, and status, with each field explained.

OpenID Connect and OAuth. Authorize requests, callbacks (query, form_post, and fragment responses visible in redirects), token requests and responses, discovery, JWKS, UserInfo, logout, PAR, introspection, and revocation. ID and access tokens are decoded with claim explanations, issued and expiry times relative to the capture and to now, and Keycloak realm and client roles.

Signature verification without fetching keys. JWTs signed with RS, PS, ES, or EdDSA algorithms are verified against the JWKS the app fetched in the same login flow, or a JWKS you paste. SAML XML signatures and redirect-binding query signatures are verified against a certificate or metadata you paste, or against SAML metadata captured in the trace. Captured metadata is only used after you click Trust, because a key is only as trustworthy as where it came from.

Findings. Each flow is checked for the mistakes we see most often: missing PKCE, state, or nonce; the implicit flow; a redirect_uri that differs between the authorize, callback, and token requests; state and nonce mismatches; SAML Destination, ACS, Recipient, and Audience mismatches; assertions that were already expired or not yet valid when captured, which usually means clock skew; unsigned assertions; SHA-1 signatures; and OAuth and SAML error codes in plain English. When Keycloak is involved, Login Tracer recognizes realm, identity-brokering, and login-action endpoints and names the setting to check, such as Valid Redirect URIs, the Name ID format, Client signature required, or PKCE enforcement.

Private by design​

Login Tracer reads the inspected tab's network log through the DevTools extension API. That API is available to any DevTools extension without a permission, and only while DevTools is open on that tab. So the manifest declares no permissions, no host permissions, no content scripts, and no background worker, and Chrome shows no permission warning when you install it. The extension cannot see other tabs, pages where DevTools is closed, or your browsing history.

It also makes no network requests of its own. The extension's Content Security Policy sets connect-src 'none', so even a bug could not send a token anywhere, and the source is linted to forbid fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSockets, and beacons. There is no telemetry, no analytics, and no account. Keys for signature checks come from what you paste or what the page already downloaded, and captured traces are discarded when you close DevTools.

Sometimes you do need to share a trace, with a colleague or in a support ticket. Export… creates a JSON file on your machine, optionally with a sanitized HAR. Cookies, Authorization headers, passwords, client secrets, PKCE verifiers, refresh tokens, and token and SAML signatures are always removed, and you can also mask user identifiers or drop token and SAML contents entirely. The dialog shows how many values were removed and a full preview of the file before you save it.

The Login Tracer privacy policy has the details.

What it can and cannot see​

Login Tracer sees what the DevTools network log sees: navigations, redirects, form posts, and requests made by the page. Open DevTools before you start the login and turn on Preserve log in the Network panel so redirects across page loads are kept. It cannot see requests made before DevTools was opened, logins in a popup or another tab (open DevTools there), or server-to-server calls such as a confidential client's back-end token exchange. Encrypted SAML assertions are not decrypted, and HMAC-signed tokens cannot be verified without the shared secret.

Try it​

Login Tracer is free. Install it from the Chrome Web Store via the Login Tracer page, which also covers setup and common questions. It is also available for Firefox 140 and later from Firefox Add-ons. If you already have a message or token in hand, our free browser-based developer tools decode SAML, JWTs, certificates, and JWKS, and run OIDC flows, without installing anything.

item.title: Keycloak 26.8.2: 33 CVEs and a Critical SAML Bypass
item.description: Keycloak 26.8.2 fixes 33 CVEs, one a critical unauthenticated SAML signature bypass. The 26.6.9 and 26.4.18 backports leave that one out. Upgrade now if you use SAML.
item.content:encoded:
Bottom line: upgrade now if Keycloak terminates or brokers SAML; within the week otherwise. Keycloak 26.8.2 fixes 33 CVEs. The one that should move your schedule is critical and needs no credentials — a signature bypass in the SAML HTTP-Redirect binding that upstream describes as leading to full account takeover of federated users. The harder problem is that 26 of the 33 have no published advisory yet, so most of this release carries no severity you can plan against.

That 33 is upstream's Security fixes list counted entry by entry; 36 CVE ids appear in the notes, three cited only as earlier issues this release repairs.

Should you upgrade?​

If you…When
Terminate or broker SAML over the HTTP-Redirect bindingNow. CVE-2026-117691, CVSS 9.1, no authentication needed
Run 26.8.0 or 26.8.1 with organizations enabledNow. Account takeover through identity-first login, reproduced on 26.8.1
Expose any realm endpoint to the internetThis week. Five denial-of-service fixes, four of them unauthenticated, one a single-request JVM kill
Allow Dynamic Client RegistrationThis week. Four fixes for protocol mappers that forge sub, aud, azp or role claims
Run 26.6 or 26.4Take the backport now, but it leaves out the critical SAML fix. See below
Run 26.7No patch. The branch is end of life. See below

Budget time for it. 26.8.2 ships fourteen breaking changes — most of them the hardening behind these CVEs.

The fix that should move your schedule​

CVE-2026-117691 / GHSA-c85j-3hq2-q6wj, critical, CVSS 9.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N). Keycloak processed percent-encoded query parameter names — %53AMLResponse — while signature verification matched only literal ones. An attacker supplies a crafted unsigned SAML message and the server acts on it instead of the signed one.

This is the second verification bypass in the same code path in two releases: 26.8.1 fixed the variant that abused ; as a parameter separator. If you deferred that upgrade you are carrying both. Any realm with a SAML identity provider or a SAML client on the redirect binding is exposed; OIDC-only realms are not.

The advisory went up the same day as the release and carries no affected-version data, so treat "every 26.8.x before 26.8.2" as the working assumption and read it directly.

The other critical is a library, not a Keycloak control​

CVE-2026-111497 / GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35 is the Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write ("Node2Shell"), rated critical 9.8 with an EPSS of 0.83. Both numbers describe Google Brotli 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, not Keycloak — the fixed versions in that advisory are 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1, which are Brotli releases, not Keycloak ones. Keycloak's own exposure is not separately rated.

Keycloak did not upgrade the library. It excluded brotli4j from the Quarkus HTTP paths (#54333), removing the decoder from the distribution. The published sources do not settle whether an unauthenticated request could reach it before — read the advisory.

Security fixes​

Seven of the 33 have a published advisory:

CVE / advisorySeverityWhat it is
CVE-2026-117691 / GHSA-c85j-3hq2-q6wjcritical 9.1SAML redirect binding acts on an unsigned message
CVE-2026-111497 / GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35critical 9.8Brotli decoder overflow — the library, not a Keycloak control
CVE-2026-96448 / GHSA-x6m6-7qg7-7r64medium 6.6FGAP v2 role check ignores composites, so a limited admin can assign realm-admin
CVE-2026-92358 / GHSA-prm3-wvj6-64vxmedium 6.4Account-link proof survives unlink; the external IdP can relink silently
CVE-2026-107889 / GHSA-gv8g-wx99-6r59medium 5.5Stored XSS on the login page via a kcSanitize bypass
CVE-2026-105305 / GHSA-ggxp-hq23-v84fmedium 5.4Device Authorization Grant ignores minimum.acr.value, bypassing MFA
CVE-2026-107623 / GHSA-qxj8-968q-qm7wmedium 4.3A DCR update silently disables offline token revocation on backchannel logout

The other 26 have no advisory, so they carry no severity and we will not estimate one. Their titles are not reassuring — account takeover via an authentication race, a missing Admin API audience check, UMA cross-owner resource access — but a title is not a rating. Read the issues from the release notes and judge your own exposure. "Unrated" is a gap in the public record, not a verdict either way.

If you run 26.7, 26.6 or 26.4​

Updated 2026-11-06: 26.6 and 26.4 backports are out

When this was published no backport existed. Upstream has since tagged 26.6.8 and 26.6.9 and 26.4.17 and 26.4.18, without release notes, and we have built images for all four. Neither branch has the critical SAML fix, CVE-2026-117691.

There are no release notes for the backports, so we matched each of the 33 fixes to upstream commits on the release branches. The result:

BranchImageOf the 33 fixesMissing
26.826.8.2all 33none
26.626.6.929CVE-2026-117691 (critical SAML bypass), plus three we could not match to a commit: CVE-2026-107623, CVE-2026-112201, CVE-2026-96457
26.426.4.1814CVE-2026-117691, the Admin API audience check, the organization SSO_AUTH takeover, the FGAP v2 composite fix, the Device Grant ACR fix, the stored XSS and 13 more
26.726.7.5noneall 33. 26.7 is end of life

26.6.9 is 26.6.8 with only the version number changed, and 26.4.18 adds one client-policy fix on top of 26.4.17, so take the newer tag on each branch. The backports ship the hardening that goes with their fixes, so check the breaking changes below. On 26.6 nearly all of them apply, including the Admin API audience check. On 26.4 the SAML broker, SOAP, DCR mapper and verified-email changes apply.

If you use SAML on 26.6 or 26.4, the backport is not enough. It does include the SAML 1.1 and SOAP denial-of-service fixes, the issuer check and the holder-of-key check, but the redirect-binding signature bypass is open on both branches. Either move to 26.8.2 or stop accepting SAML over the HTTP-Redirect binding until upstream backports the fix. Upstream gives no date for that, and the advisory still has no affected-version data.

On 26.7 nothing has changed. release/26.7 is archived, so 26.8.2 is the only patched path.

All tags live on quay.io/phasetwo/keycloak, including the backports upstream tags but never announces.

Breaking changes and migration​

Fourteen, which is a lot for a patch. The ones most likely to break you:

  • The Admin REST API enforces an audience check through a new kc-admin-api client scope (CVE-2026-19688). Service accounts calling the Admin API need it.
  • Protocol mapper management via the Admin API is restricted to realm administrators, and client registration policies limit mapper types, default roles and full scope.
  • SAML 1.1 request parsing is off by default; SOAP endpoints cap requests at 120,000 bytes.
  • The SAML broker requires a valid bearer subject confirmation and rejects ProxyRestriction assertions, and the SAML adapter validates the IdP issuer.
  • Token exchange tokens can no longer outlive the subject token.
  • IdP auto-linking requires a verified email (CVE-2026-97175), as does organization domain-based membership.

The official release notes still stop at 26.8.0; all fourteen are in the migration changes.

How to upgrade​

Rehearse the Admin API scope and SAML broker changes on staging; both fail quietly. Our production checklist covers the exposure questions above, and self-service upgrades covers the mechanics.

Our managed Keycloak clusters are patched in our maintenance windows, under SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001. Talk to us if you would rather not schedule this one yourself.

item.title: The CLOUD Act and your identity provider
item.description: What the CLOUD Act does and does not reach when your identity provider has a US parent, which legal process gets which Keycloak data, tested on 26.8.1.
item.content:encoded:
The CLOUD Act does not hand anyone a key to a European data centre. It does something narrower, and for an identity provider more awkward than the usual telling. 18 U.S.C. § 2713 makes the location of data irrelevant to whether a provider under US jurisdiction has to produce it, and the process that reaches most of what an identity provider holds is the cheapest instrument in the Stored Communications Act: a subpoena for subscriber records, no warrant, no judicial finding, and no obligation to tell the customer. Below is what the statute says, which level of process reaches which table in a Keycloak realm (tested on 26.8.1), why the defence the CLOUD Act added does not cover an EU customer's identity data on either of its two conditions, and what a vendor with a US parent can honestly promise. Including us.

This is an engineering and procurement read of public legal texts, not legal advice. Where something is contested, it says so.

What the CLOUD Act actually changed in 2018​

The Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act did two things. It added § 2713 to the Stored Communications Act, which reads in full:

A provider of electronic communication service or remote computing service shall comply with the obligations of this chapter to preserve, backup, or disclose the contents of a wire or electronic communication and any record or other information pertaining to a customer or subscriber within such provider's possession, custody, or control, regardless of whether such communication, record, or other information is located within or outside of the United States.

And it added § 2523, a framework for executive agreements with foreign governments, plus a new motion to quash in § 2703(h) for providers caught between two legal systems.

What it did not do is create a new power to collect anything. The orders are still the ordinary ones in § 2703, written in 1986. The CLOUD Act settled the question those orders had left open, which the government had just lost in the Second Circuit over a mailbox in Dublin: whether a US order reaches data the provider happens to store abroad. The answer is that storage location is not the test. Possession, custody, or control is the test.

Two consequences follow for anyone buying hosted identity. A region setting answers a question the statute declines to ask. And because the test is about the provider rather than the data, the analysis turns on corporate structure and operational access, which is the subject of data residency vs data sovereignty for your identity provider.

Three levels of process, and which one reaches an IdP​

The SCA is a tiered statute. What the government must obtain depends on what it is asking for, not on how sensitive you think the data is.

InstrumentStatuteStandardWhat it reaches
Warrant§ 2703(a), (b)Probable cause, judgeContents of a wire or electronic communication
Court order§ 2703(d)"Specific and articulable facts" showing relevanceAny non-content record about a subscriber
Subpoena§ 2703(c)(2)Administrative or grand jury subpoena; no judgeA specific enumerated list, below

The list in § 2703(c)(2) is the one to read closely, because it is the only category obtainable without a court looking at the request at all. A provider must disclose the:

(A) name; (B) address; (C) local and long distance telephone connection records, or records of session times and durations; (D) length of service (including start date) and types of service utilized; (E) telephone or instrument number or other subscriber number or identity, including any temporarily assigned network address; and (F) means and source of payment for such service

Then § 2703(c)(3): "A governmental entity receiving records or information under this subsection is not required to provide notice to a subscriber or customer."

Read that enumeration again with a login system in mind. Session times and durations. A temporarily assigned network address. Start date and type of service. It was drafted for telephone billing records and dial-up accounts. It describes an identity provider's primary data model almost field for field.

What those categories look like against a real realm​

Everything below ran on a stock Keycloak 26.8.1 against PostgreSQL 17, with one user, one client, three successful logins and one failed one:

docker run -d --name kc --network kcnet --memory 1536m -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin \
  -e KC_DB=postgres -e KC_DB_URL="jdbc:postgresql://pg:5432/keycloak" \
  -e KC_DB_USERNAME=kc -e KC_DB_PASSWORD=kcpass \
  quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.1 start-dev

The subscriber record, through the administrative API a customer uses:

$ kcadm.sh get users/f1261d8f-... -r eu-demo
{
  "id" : "f1261d8f-6a11-43c5-813a-d2d7634eea72",
  "username" : "anja.k",
  "firstName" : "Anja",
  "lastName" : "Kowalski",
  "email" : "anja.kowalski@example.de",
  "emailVerified" : false,
  "enabled" : true,
  "createdTimestamp" : 1793610882190
}

createdTimestamp is § 2703(c)(2)(D), length of service including start date, sitting in a field by itself.

Sessions are the part most people assume are ephemeral. They are not. persistent-user-sessions is a supported feature enabled by default in current Keycloak, so an online session is a database row, and it survives a restart:

$ psql -U kc -d keycloak -c "SELECT user_session_id, offline_flag,
    data::json->>'ipAddress' AS ip_address,
    to_timestamp(created_on) AS created,
    to_timestamp(last_session_refresh) AS last_refresh
  FROM offline_user_session WHERE user_id = (SELECT id FROM user_entity WHERE username='anja.k');"

     user_session_id      | offline_flag | ip_address |        created         |      last_refresh
--------------------------+--------------+------------+------------------------+------------------------
 lBxvFPTvlf7ivgKUpWvSMi6A |            0 | 172.18.0.1 | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00 | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00
 nxYnop4FGJIoseD5t7sIudRH |            0 | 172.18.0.1 | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00 | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00
 KocEVFq5b9fgEwwZk3tjxedG |            1 | 172.18.0.1 | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00 | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00

The table is named for offline sessions and holds both; offline_flag = 0 is an ordinary online session. created and last_session_refresh, bounded by the realm's idle and maximum lifespans — 1,800 and 36,000 seconds by default — are records of session times and durations. The IP address is in the row.

The event store is the same shape and longer-lived:

$ psql -U kc -d keycloak -c "SELECT type, to_timestamp(event_time/1000) AS at, ip_address, error
                             FROM event_entity ORDER BY event_time;"
    type     |           at           | ip_address |          error
-------------+------------------------+------------+--------------------------
 LOGIN       | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00 | 172.18.0.1 |
 LOGIN       | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00 | 172.18.0.1 |
 LOGIN       | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00 | 172.18.0.1 |
 LOGIN_ERROR | 2026-11-02 09:14:48+00 | 172.18.0.1 | invalid_user_credentials

A realm with events enabled and no eventsExpiration set keeps those rows indefinitely, which makes retention a decision you have already made by not making it. The mechanics are in user events in Keycloak and how we scaled Keycloak event storage.

So the mapping, category by category:

§ 2703(c)(2)Where it is in a Keycloak realmReachable by subpoena alone
(A) nameuser_entity.first_name, last_name, usernameYes
(B) addressEmail, and any address attribute the realm definesYes
(C) records of session times and durationsoffline_user_session.created_on, last_session_refreshYes
(D) length of service, start date, type of serviceuser_entity.created_timestamp; client and protocol per sessionYes
(E) subscriber identity, temporarily assigned network addressuser_entity.id, and ipAddress on every session and eventYes
(F) means and source of paymentNot in Keycloak. In whatever billing system you runNot from the IdP

What is left for a warrant is thin. An identity provider is not a mailbox: it does not store the contents of your users' communications, it stores facts about them and about when they signed in. Almost everything of value in it falls on the records side of the line, which is the side with the lowest bar and no notice requirement.

The credential store is the one genuine limit, and it is cryptographic rather than legal:

$ psql -U kc -d keycloak -c "SELECT c.type, left(c.secret_data,34) AS secret_data, c.credential_data
                             FROM credential c JOIN user_entity u ON u.id=c.user_id
                             WHERE u.username='anja.k';"
   type   |            secret_data             |                          credential_data
----------+------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------
 password | {"value":"ive1qXfpydxQKbca/h08A656 | {"hashIterations":5,"algorithm":"argon2","additionalParameters":
                                               |  {"hashLength":["32"],"memory":["7168"],"type":["id"],
                                               |   "version":["1.3"],"parallelism":["1"]}}

Compelled production of that row yields an argon2id digest, not a password. It also yields nothing about what the account can do that the role and group tables do not say more directly. Note the asymmetry worth knowing about: the administrative API masks secret_data and the database does not, which is the same gap, in a different column, as the signing-key export demonstrated in the residency and sovereignty post.

Two caveats, because this mapping is an argument and not a holding. The line between "contents" and "a record" has been litigated for forty years and is not crisp at the edges. And whether a business-to-business managed identity service is even a provider of "remote computing service" is itself a live question, since § 2711(2) defines that as "the provision to the public of computer storage or processing services". If a provider falls outside the definition, the SCA's tiers do not apply to it and the government uses an ordinary grand jury subpoena against the company instead. That is a different route to the same place, not a shelter.

The defence the CLOUD Act added, and why it misses you​

Section 2703(h) is the part of the Act that was sold as the protection for foreign customers. A provider may move to quash within 14 days of service where it reasonably believes both that the subscriber is not a US person and does not reside in the US, and that disclosure "would create a material risk that the provider would violate the laws of a qualifying foreign government".

A qualifying foreign government, per § 2703(h)(1)(A), is one "with which the United States has an executive agreement that has entered into force under section 2523".

As of 2 November 2026 the Department of Justice's own CLOUD Act page lists exactly two such agreements, with the United Kingdom (signed 3 October 2019, in force 3 October 2022) and Australia. For the European Union it lists a 2019 joint statement opening negotiations and a 3 March 2023 announcement that negotiations had resumed, and no agreement. No EU member state has one individually.

So for an EU customer's identity data the statutory motion fails twice over. It fails on subject matter, because § 2703(h)(2)(A) is written for "the contents of a wire or electronic communication" and the material at issue is records. And it fails on the foreign government, because the GDPR is not the law of a qualifying foreign government within the meaning of the section. What is left is the ordinary common-law comity argument that providers made before 2018, which is available, slower, and entirely dependent on the provider's willingness to spend money on it.

This is worth stating plainly because it inverts the usual pitch. The CLOUD Act's own safety valve was built for the UK arrangement, and it is the UK leg of a structure like ours, not the EU leg, that it was designed to relieve.

What EU law compels, in the other direction​

A European buyer evaluating US legal exposure in isolation is measuring one side of a vice.

The UK–US Data Access Agreement works both ways: US authorities can serve qualifying serious-crime orders directly on UK providers, and UK authorities on US providers, with each side barred from targeting the other's persons. And since 18 August 2026, Regulation (EU) 2023/1543 has applied — the e-Evidence Regulation, under which a judicial authority in one member state can serve a European Production Order directly on a service provider offering services in the Union, with a ten-day deadline and eight hours in an emergency.

Against that sits Article 48 GDPR, "Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law", which says that a third-country court judgment or administrative decision requiring a controller or processor to disclose personal data "may only be recognised or enforceable in any manner if based on an international agreement, such as a mutual legal assistance treaty, in force between the requesting third country and the Union or a Member State".

A US order compelling production of EU identity data and Article 48 point in opposite directions, and there is no EU–US executive agreement to reconcile them. That unresolved conflict is the actual risk a DPO is asking you about. It is not solved by hosting in Frankfurt, and it is not solved by a vendor's assurances either. It is a gap in the treaty layer that providers sit inside.

This is not the statute most people mean​

Two different things get argued under one name, and separating them improves every conversation that follows.

The CLOUD Act route is criminal process. There is a specific case, a named target, a court somewhere in the chain, and a defined list of what may be produced. A provider can see it, log it, challenge it, and in most circumstances tell you about it.

Foreign-intelligence collection under FISA Section 702 is a different regime, programmatic rather than case-by-case, directed at non-US persons abroad, and accompanied by secrecy obligations that make provider transparency largely unavailable. Section 702's statutory authority lapsed in June 2026 and, as of 2 November 2026, Congress has not reauthorised it; collection continues under Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court certifications approved in March 2026 and valid until 17 March 2027. A lapsed statute is not a dead programme. Anyone who tells you Section 702 "expired" and stops there is giving you the half of the sentence that sells.

What actually moves the analysis​

Since the test is possession, custody or control, the only interventions that change anything are the ones that change what the provider can technically or organisationally obtain. In rough order of how much they matter for an identity provider:

  1. Who can read the realm signing keys. Whoever can read them can mint a valid token for any user, which makes key custody the highest-leverage control in the system.
  2. Who can reach the control plane, from where, under what approval, and whether that access is logged.
  3. Which legal entity is your counterparty, where it is incorporated, and whether the relationship with any non-EU parent is a real organisational separation or an org chart.
  4. What the data model keeps at all. Retention you have set is data that cannot be produced, because it no longer exists. See the DPO checklist for SaaS authentication for the version of this a procurement team will send you.
  5. Region, last, because it is the control that changes the least and is quoted the most.

A corporate structure by itself insulates nothing. Courts apply a "legal right or practical ability" test to data held by affiliates, and a parent is routinely treated as controlling a subsidiary's data. The honest question to put to any vendor is not "where is it hosted" but "what could you actually hand over if you were ordered to, and who inside your company could execute that".

The quote your buyer will bring you​

On 10 June 2025, before the French Senate's commission of inquiry into public procurement and digital sovereignty, the rapporteur asked Anton Carniaux, director of public and legal affairs at Microsoft France, under oath, whether he could guarantee that French citizens' data entrusted to Microsoft would never be transmitted to the US government without the explicit agreement of the French authorities. The answer, from the official record:

« Non, je ne peux pas le garantir, mais, encore une fois, cela ne s'est encore jamais produit. »

"No, I cannot guarantee it, but, once again, it has never yet happened."

Earlier in the same hearing, on what happens when an order is legally founded: « Lorsque nous sommes obligés de les donner, nous les donnons. » When we are obliged to hand them over, we hand them over.

Quote it with the caveat. Both halves are true, and the second half is the one that gets dropped by whichever side is quoting it. The answer applies to us in exactly the same way, which is why we would rather write it here than have you find it in a risk assessment.

Where we stand​

Our parent, Phase Two, Inc., is incorporated in the United States, so we cannot and do not claim to be beyond the reach of § 2713. Your counterparty for EU and UK business is Phase Two UK, Ltd, registered in England and Wales, company number 16815578; the European Commission renewed its adequacy decision for the United Kingdom on 19 December 2025. Identity data for an EU cluster is stored and processed in Frankfurt with the standing backup in Ireland and is not replicated outside the EU, while our control plane runs in the US and our engineers are distributed globally, so administrative access to an EU cluster can come from outside the EU. That is a restricted transfer and we disclose it rather than discover it with you. Realm signing keys for EU clusters are held in our key management service in the Frankfurt region; they are our keys in our KMS, and we do not offer bring-your-own-key on hosted clusters today. We are not certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework and do not rely on it.

What we do when a demand arrives — route it to one place, verify it, push it back to you as controller, challenge what is overbroad, notify you unless prohibited, disclose the minimum, publish the count — is written out on our government requests page, along with the count itself, which is still zero. The per-class map of what lives where is in where your Keycloak data lives, and the region list is in the regions documentation.

If none of that is sufficient for your risk profile, that is a legitimate conclusion rather than an objection to handle, and running upstream Keycloak yourself remains the answer we would give you. We would rather you ran it somewhere we do not host it than bought a promise from us that no company shaped like ours can keep.

The full map, the subprocessor list and the transfer mechanisms are on the EU data residency page, which is also where our managed Keycloak regions are described. The Article 28 terms, including the subprocessor objection right and the breach notification window, are on the data processing agreement page.

Keycloak behaviour was tested on 26.8.1 with PostgreSQL 17 on 2 November 2026, against the 26.8 server administration and features documentation. Legal texts were verified the same day against primary sources: 18 U.S.C. §§ 2703, 2711 and 2713 as published by the US Government Publishing Office; Article 48 GDPR; Regulation (EU) 2023/1543 and its 18 August 2026 application date; the Department of Justice's CLOUD Act resources page for the list of executive agreements in force; the European Commission's adequacy decisions page for the UK and EU–US decisions; and the Sénat's official compte rendu of the 10 June 2025 hearing for the quotations. The status of FISA Section 702 was checked against reporting and the Brennan Center's explainer as last updated 16 October 2026; nothing had been enacted as of 2 November 2026. Whether a particular record is "content" or "a record", and whether a given service is a "remote computing service", are questions courts decide case by case.

item.title: Porting Azure AD B2C custom policies to Keycloak
item.description: A concept-by-concept map from Azure AD B2C custom policies (IEF) to Keycloak 26.8 — user journeys, technical profiles, claims transformations — and the three things that need Java.
item.content:encoded:
Most of an Azure AD B2C custom policy maps onto Keycloak configuration rather than code. A user journey becomes an authentication flow, orchestration steps become executions, preconditions become conditional subflows, the claims schema becomes the declarative user profile, and page layouts become themes. None of that is Java.

Three things are not configuration. RESTful technical profiles called mid-journey become a custom Authenticator. Long claims-transformation chains become either several protocol mappers or one script mapper — and the script mapper is a JAR you build, not JavaScript you paste into the console, which surprises people. And orchestration that branches on a computed value rather than on the presence of a claim has no declarative equivalent at all.

Everything below was run against Keycloak 26.8.1 in start-dev. The Java compiles against 26.8.1; every HTTP status and response body is copied from an actual run.

The short version​

Azure AD B2CKeycloak 26.8Code?
<UserJourney>Authentication flowNo
<OrchestrationStep>Execution, or a subflowNo
<Precondition>CONDITIONAL subflow + a condition executionNo
Self-asserted technical profileBuilt-in form authenticator + user profileNo
OIDC/SAML technical profileIdentity providerNo
AAD read/write technical profileKeycloak's own user storeNo
RESTful technical profileAuthenticator SPIYes
<ClaimsSchema> / <ClaimType>Declarative user profileNo
<ClaimsTransformation>Protocol mapperNo
Chained transformationsScript mapper (a deployed JAR)Yes
<ContentDefinition> / LoadUriKeycloak themeNo
<LocalizedResources>Theme message bundlesNo
<RelyingParty> output claimsClient scopes + protocol mappersNo

Work down that table against your own TrustFrameworkExtensions.xml before estimating anything. The count of rows in the "Yes" column is your project.

User journeys become authentication flows​

A B2C user journey is an ordered list of orchestration steps, each referencing a technical profile, each optionally guarded by a precondition. A Keycloak authentication flow is an ordered list of executions, each referencing an authenticator, each with a requirement, and subflows can be guarded by conditions. The shapes match closely enough that you can usually transcribe one into the other on paper first.

Built-in flows are read-only, so you start by copying one:

kcadm.sh create authentication/flows/browser/copy -r b2c -s newName=b2c-journey

Then add a subflow for each orchestration step that needs a guard, and the executions inside it:

# The orchestration step
kcadm.sh create authentication/flows/b2c-journey/executions/flow -r b2c \
  -s alias=step-mfa -s type=basic-flow -s provider=registration-page-form \
  -s description='OrchestrationStep with Precondition'

# Its precondition, then the technical profile it guards
kcadm.sh create authentication/flows/step-mfa/executions/execution -r b2c \
  -s provider=conditional-user-attribute
kcadm.sh create authentication/flows/step-mfa/executions/execution -r b2c \
  -s provider=auth-otp-form

Read the flow back and you get this — the copied browser flow with the new subflow at the bottom:

Cookie                                       ALTERNATIVE  auth-cookie
Kerberos                                     DISABLED     auth-spnego
Identity Provider Redirector                 ALTERNATIVE  identity-provider-redirector
b2c-journey Organization                     ALTERNATIVE  -
  b2c-journey Browser - Conditional Organization CONDITIONAL  -
    Condition - user configured                  REQUIRED     conditional-user-configured
    Organization Identity-First Login            ALTERNATIVE  organization
b2c-journey forms                            ALTERNATIVE  -
  Username Password Form                       REQUIRED     auth-username-password-form
  b2c-journey Browser - Conditional 2FA        CONDITIONAL  -
    Condition - user configured                  REQUIRED     conditional-user-configured
    Condition - credential                       REQUIRED     conditional-credential
    OTP Form                                     ALTERNATIVE  auth-otp-form
    WebAuthn Authenticator                       DISABLED     webauthn-authenticator
    Recovery Authentication Code Form            DISABLED     auth-recovery-authn-code-form
step-mfa                                     DISABLED     -
  Condition - user attribute                   DISABLED     conditional-user-attribute
  OTP Form                                     DISABLED     auth-otp-form

Two things in that output matter. The first is that everything you just created arrived DISABLED — Keycloak does not infer a requirement from the fact that you added an execution, and a flow that silently does nothing is the usual first failure. The second is that the stock flow already demonstrates the pattern you want: a CONDITIONAL subflow whose first children are conditions and whose remaining children only run if they pass.

Set the requirements as a separate step. The requirement model has four values and some non-obvious interactions between them — building a custom authentication flow walks through the five ways it fails quietly, which is worth reading before you transcribe a twelve-step journey.

Preconditions become conditions​

B2C preconditions come in two useful flavours: ClaimsExist and ClaimEquals, with ExecuteActionsIf inverting them. Keycloak ships seven condition executions, and this is the complete list on 26.8.1:

conditional-client-scope
conditional-credential
conditional-level-of-authentication
conditional-sub-flow-executed
conditional-user-attribute
conditional-user-configured
conditional-user-role

The mapping is mostly direct. ClaimsExist on a user attribute is conditional-user-attribute. ClaimEquals is the same condition with a value configured. A precondition on whether the user has MFA set up is conditional-user-configured. A precondition on the requested authentication context is conditional-level-of-authentication. A precondition that depends on an earlier step having run is conditional-sub-flow-executed.

What is not there is a condition on an arbitrary expression. If your precondition tests a claim produced by a transformation two steps earlier, there is no declarative equivalent — you either persist the value as a user attribute first and test it with conditional-user-attribute, or you write a condition in Java. Persisting it is almost always the better answer, because it is also the thing that makes the journey debuggable.

The claims schema becomes the declarative user profile​

A <ClaimType> with a <DataType>, a <UserInputType> and a predicate validation maps onto one attribute in the realm's user profile. This is a closer match than it first appears: Keycloak's user profile carries display names, input types, per-role view and edit permissions, required-ness, and validators.

curl -X PUT "$KC/admin/realms/b2c/users/profile" -H "$A" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
 "attributes":[
  {"name":"username","permissions":{"view":["admin","user"],"edit":["admin","user"]}},
  {"name":"email","required":{"roles":["user"]},
   "permissions":{"view":["admin","user"],"edit":["admin","user"]}},
  {"name":"firstName","permissions":{"view":["admin","user"],"edit":["admin","user"]}},
  {"name":"lastName","permissions":{"view":["admin","user"],"edit":["admin","user"]}},
  {"name":"extension_loyaltyId","displayName":"Loyalty ID","multivalued":false,
   "required":{"roles":["user"]},
   "validations":{"pattern":{"pattern":"^[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{8}$","error-message":"loyaltyId-invalid"},
                  "length":{"min":10,"max":10}},
   "permissions":{"view":["admin","user"],"edit":["admin","user"]},
   "annotations":{"inputType":"text"}}
 ]}'
# HTTP 200

The validators are enforced server-side, on the Admin API as well as on the login forms, which is the part B2C predicates do not quite give you. A user that violates the pattern is rejected with the field named:

HTTP 400
{"errors":[
  {"field":"extension_loyaltyId","errorMessage":"error-invalid-length","params":["extension_loyaltyId",10,10]},
  {"field":"extension_loyaltyId","errorMessage":"loyaltyId-invalid","params":["extension_loyaltyId","^[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{8}$"]}]}

Note that B2C's extension_ prefix is just a string here — keep the names identical to the B2C ones during the migration and rename later, if at all. Reconciling two systems is hard enough without a translation layer in the middle.

Declare every attribute before you import anything. An attribute the realm does not know about is silently discarded on write, and the write still succeeds. That behaviour and the four unmanagedAttributePolicy values are covered properly in managed vs unmanaged attributes; it is the single most expensive thing to discover late in a B2C migration.

Technical profiles: four kinds, four destinations​

"Technical profile" is one word covering four unrelated jobs. Separate them before you map them.

Self-asserted profiles collect input from the user. In Keycloak these are form authenticators plus the user profile above — the fields rendered on the login, registration and update-profile pages come from the profile configuration, so a self-asserted technical profile usually disappears into configuration you have already written.

Azure Active Directory profiles (AAD-UserReadUsingObjectId, AAD-UserWriteUsingLogonEmail and friends) read and write the B2C directory. Keycloak has its own user store, so these have no equivalent and need none. They vanish.

OpenID Connect and SAML profiles federate to another IdP. These become identity providers — configuration, one per provider, with mappers to pull claims onto the user:

kcadm.sh create identity-provider/instances -r b2c \
  -s alias=partner-idp -s providerId=oidc -s enabled=true \
  -s 'config.authorizationUrl=https://idp.example.com/authorize' \
  -s 'config.tokenUrl=https://idp.example.com/token' \
  -s 'config.jwksUrl=https://idp.example.com/keys' \
  -s 'config.useJwksUrl=true' -s 'config.clientId=...' -s 'config.clientSecret=...'

kcadm.sh create identity-provider/instances/partner-idp/mappers -r b2c \
  -s name=loyalty -s identityProviderAlias=partner-idp \
  -s identityProviderMapper=oidc-user-attribute-idp-mapper \
  -s 'config.claim=extension_loyaltyId' \
  -s 'config.user.attribute=extension_loyaltyId' \
  -s 'config.syncMode=INHERIT'

Worth pausing here, because this is where the comparison with the other destination gets sharp. Microsoft's B2C-to-External-ID migration guide says that "third-party identity providers configured through B2C custom policies aren't supported" in External ID. In Keycloak a third-party IdP is four lines of configuration and there is no supported-list to be on.

RESTful profiles are the ones that cost you. They need an authenticator.

RESTful technical profiles become an Authenticator​

A RestfulProvider technical profile called from an orchestration step does three things: send some input claims to an HTTP endpoint, receive output claims, and fail the journey on a non-success response. That is exactly an Authenticator.

The whole surface is two interfaces and a service file. Here is the core of it — the full class compiles against Keycloak 26.8.1 as a provided-scope Maven build:

@Override
public void authenticate(AuthenticationFlowContext context) {
  Map<String, String> cfg = context.getAuthenticatorConfig() == null
      ? Map.of() : context.getAuthenticatorConfig().getConfig();
  UserModel user = context.getUser();

  try {
    // InputClaims: what the technical profile would have sent.
    String body = JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(Map.of(
        "email", user.getEmail() == null ? "" : user.getEmail(),
        "objectId", user.getFirstAttribute("b2c_object_id") == null
            ? "" : user.getFirstAttribute("b2c_object_id")));

    HttpResponse<String> res = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build()
        .send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(cfg.get("endpointUrl")))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build(),
            HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

    // A technical profile that returns a conflict fails the journey. So does this.
    if (res.statusCode() == 409) {
      context.failure(AuthenticationFlowError.INVALID_USER);
      return;
    }
    if (res.statusCode() / 100 != 2) {
      // Not "the answer is no" -- "we did not get an answer". Different outcome.
      context.failure(AuthenticationFlowError.INTERNAL_ERROR);
      return;
    }

    // OutputClaims: persist what came back so a protocol mapper can emit it.
    Map<String, Object> out = JsonSerialization.readValue(res.body(), Map.class);
    Object claim = out.get(cfg.getOrDefault("outputClaim", "membershipTier"));
    if (claim != null) {
      user.setSingleAttribute(cfg.getOrDefault("outputClaim", "membershipTier"),
                              String.valueOf(claim));
    }
    context.success();
  } catch (Exception e) {
    context.failure(AuthenticationFlowError.INTERNAL_ERROR);
  }
}

The distinction in the middle is the one to copy deliberately. A 409 and a timeout are not the same result. B2C's UserMessageIfClaimsPrincipalDoesNotExist metadata encourages you to treat every non-200 as a user-facing "no"; in a flow that gates access, conflating "your API said no" with "your API did not answer" is how an outage becomes a lockout, or worse, an accidental allow.

Implement AuthenticatorFactory on the same class, expose the endpoint URL and the output claim as ProviderConfigProperty entries so the step is configurable per realm, register it in META-INF/services/org.keycloak.authentication.AuthenticatorFactory, and drop the JAR in providers/. It then appears in the execution picker next to the 42 built-in authenticators and takes per-execution configuration the way a built-in does.

Claims transformations become protocol mappers​

Most transformations are not transformations at all, they are claim plumbing, and Keycloak has 39 protocol mappers for exactly that. CopyClaim into the token is a user-attribute mapper. CreateStringClaim with a constant is a hardcoded-claim mapper.

# CopyClaim: extension_loyaltyId -> loyalty_id
kcadm.sh create clients/$CID/protocol-mappers/models -r b2c \
  -s name=loyalty-id -s protocol=openid-connect \
  -s protocolMapper=oidc-usermodel-attribute-mapper \
  -s 'config."user.attribute"=extension_loyaltyId' \
  -s 'config."claim.name"=loyalty_id' -s 'config."jsonType.label"=String' \
  -s 'config."id.token.claim"=true' -s 'config."access.token.claim"=true'

# CreateStringClaim: a constant
kcadm.sh create clients/$CID/protocol-mappers/models -r b2c \
  -s name=tenant -s protocol=openid-connect \
  -s protocolMapper=oidc-hardcoded-claim-mapper \
  -s 'config."claim.name"=tid' -s 'config."claim.value"=contoso' \
  -s 'config."jsonType.label"=String' -s 'config."id.token.claim"=true'

Both return HTTP 201. Put them on a shared client scope rather than per-client if more than one application needs the claim — that is the <RelyingParty> output-claims list, expressed once.

The script-mapper trap​

For the transformations that genuinely compute something — string formatting, conditionals, concatenating three claims into one — the documented answer is a script mapper. It does not work the way the documentation implies.

Starting Keycloak with --features=scripts and creating a script mapper through the Admin API gives you this:

HTTP 404
{"error":"ProtocolMapper provider not found"}

The feature is enabled — SCRIPTS shows up in the server's feature list — and the mapper provider still is not registered. Script mappers are deployed, not authored. You package the JavaScript in a JAR with a META-INF/keycloak-scripts.json descriptor naming it, drop the JAR in providers/, and only then does the mapper appear. There is no console path and no API path that takes a script body.

That is a reasonable security decision — arbitrary server-side JavaScript posted over the Admin API would be remote code execution with extra steps — but it changes the estimate. A script mapper is a build artifact on the same footing as the Authenticator above: same JAR, same pipeline, same release process. If you were counting on script mappers to avoid writing Java, count again; you are writing a deployable either way, and Java is easier to test.

Our practical advice is to avoid script mappers for anything you can express as a user attribute. Compute the value where it is produced — in the Authenticator that called the REST endpoint, or in the application that owns the data — persist it as an attribute, and emit it with a plain attribute mapper. It is debuggable, it survives upgrades, and it does not need a feature flag.

Page layouts become themes​

B2C's <ContentDefinition> points LoadUri at HTML you host, and B2C injects its form into a container element. Keycloak inverts this: you override the templates themselves. Keycloak 26.8 has six theme types:

account  admin  common  email  login  welcome

The login theme is the one that corresponds to your content definitions, and email picks up the verification and password-reset messages that B2C sends through a third-party provider via custom policy. <LocalizedResources> becomes message bundles — messages_en.properties, messages_de.properties — in the same theme.

This is more capable than what you have, and it is also more work, because you are theming real templates rather than styling an injected form. Do not schedule the theme work inside the migration window. Ship with a lightly branded stock theme, cut over, then do the design pass. The one thing to get right on day one is the email theme, because those messages go to users during cutover.

What genuinely has no equivalent​

Three things, and they are the honest answer to "can we automate this".

Orchestration that branches on computed values. Covered above: persist the value, then condition on it, or write a condition authenticator.

<ValidationTechnicalProfile> chains. B2C lets a self-asserted profile validate its input by running another technical profile, which can itself call REST and fail with a specific user-facing message. Keycloak's equivalent is a form authenticator that does the validation inline and re-renders the form with an error, which means the validation and the form are one class rather than two composable pieces. Each chain is a small amount of Java.

The IEF claims-transformation library itself. There are dozens of transformation methods, and Keycloak does not ship equivalents as a library. Most translate to nothing, because the work moves somewhere better. The ones that do not become code.

There is also no converter, from anyone, in either direction. Microsoft's own migration guide maps custom policies to External ID's custom authentication extensions as a concept, with no tooling. Treat any claim of an automated IEF migration with suspicion.

How long this takes​

Estimate off the table at the top, not off the number of policy files — a tenant with six policy files inheriting from one base is usually less work than a tenant with two that each call three REST endpoints.

Your tenantRough effort
Built-in user flows only, no custom policiesDays. There is nothing to port
Custom policies, no REST profiles, no transformation chainsOne to two weeks of configuration
Custom policies with two or three REST profilesAdd a week per endpoint, including tests
Enterprise federation through custom policiesA few days per IdP, mostly spent on the other side
The lot, plus a bespoke themeTwo to four months end to end

Those are ranges, not quotes. The variance is almost entirely in the REST profiles and in how much undocumented behaviour your policies encode.

Do this next​

Export your policy files and count three things: orchestration steps, technical profiles by protocol, and distinct claims transformations. That takes an hour with grep and it is the only input anyone needs to give you a real estimate.

grep -c '<OrchestrationStep' TrustFrameworkExtensions.xml
grep -o 'Protocol Name="[A-Za-z]*"' TrustFrameworkExtensions.xml | sort | uniq -c
grep -o 'TransformationMethod="[A-Za-z]*"' TrustFrameworkExtensions.xml | sort | uniq -c

Then stand up Keycloak 26.8.1 locally and transcribe your simplest journey — usually sign-up or sign-in — end to end. A day on the simplest one tells you more than a week of planning on the hardest, and it is the only way to find out which of your preconditions test computed values.

The surrounding decisions — whether to move at all, and where — are in what Azure AD B2C's end of sale actually means, and the side-by-side is on Keycloak vs. Azure AD B2C.
