If you would rather hand the policy files to someone who has read a few of them, talk to us about migrating to Keycloak — and if you want the result run for you afterwards, that is managed Keycloak.

item.title: Keycloak slow migration vs fast migration: moving your users
item.description: Slow (lazy, just-in-time) and fast (bulk) user migration to Keycloak — how each works, which GitHub repo to use for slow migration, how to import password hashes for a fast one, and how to combine them.
item.content:encoded:
A slow migration moves users from a legacy system into Keycloak one at a time, as each of them logs in. It goes by other names too: lazy migration, just-in-time (JIT) migration, trickle migration. Nobody gets a password reset email, there is no cutover weekend, and users who never come back are never migrated.

The other side is a fast migration: a bulk import that moves every user into Keycloak at once, before or at cutover. It is quicker to finish and easier to reason about, but it needs something a slow migration doesn't, usually the users' password hashes.

Keycloak doesn't ship slow migration. You add it with a user storage provider, and the one almost everyone uses is open source on GitHub: daniel-frak/keycloak-user-migration. This post covers how slow and fast migrations work, where the code lives, how to choose, and how to combine the two so a slow migration doesn't drag on for months.

Slow migrationFast migration
When users moveOne at a time, at their next loginAll at once, at import
Password hashes neededNo, the legacy system checks passwordsYes, or users set a new password
Legacy system after cutoverMust stay up and answer the migration endpointsCan be turned off
Dormant usersNever migrated unless you add a final stepMigrated with everyone else
Time to finishWeeks to months, plus a long tailHours to days

Not the same as a slow Keycloak upgrade​

Searching for "Keycloak slow migration" also turns up a different problem: the database schema migration Keycloak runs when you upgrade it, which can take a long time on large realms. That is a version upgrade, not a user migration, and it is out of scope here. If that is what you're dealing with, see Upgrading. The rest of this post is about moving users from another system into Keycloak.

How slow migration works​

Keycloak's user storage SPI lets Keycloak ask an external system about a user it has never seen. The migration provider turns that into two HTTP endpoints that you add to your legacy system:

  1. A user types their username and password into the Keycloak login page.
  2. Keycloak doesn't know the user, so the provider calls GET {your-url}/{username}. Your legacy system returns the user's profile: email, name, attributes, roles, groups, and optionally TOTP devices and organizations.
  3. The provider calls POST {your-url}/{username} with {"password": "..."}. Your legacy system checks the password against its own hash and returns 200 if it's correct.
  4. Keycloak creates the user, hashes the password with its own algorithm (Argon2 by default), and logs them in.
  5. On every later login, Keycloak authenticates the user locally. The legacy system isn't called again.

Because your legacy system checks the password, you never need to export password hashes, and you never need Keycloak to understand the old hashing scheme. That is the main reason to choose a slow migration: many identity providers, Okta and Azure AD B2C among them, won't give you the hashes at all.

The GitHub repos​

RepoWhat it is
daniel-frak/keycloak-user-migrationThe upstream plugin. Releases are versioned per Keycloak major version (6.x for Keycloak 26). Start here if you self-host.
legacy-system-exampleA sample legacy service in the same repo that implements both endpoints. Useful for seeing the exact request and response shapes.
p2-inc/keycloak-user-migrationPhase Two's fork, which we keep in step with upstream. It's installed on every Phase Two cluster, so managed customers don't need to build or deploy anything.
p2-inc/workos-keycloak-migratorA worked example of a complete migration off WorkOS, including a bridge that serves the two endpoints.

To install the upstream plugin on a self-hosted Keycloak, download the release jar that matches your Keycloak major version, put it in the providers directory, and run kc.sh build. If you run the Phase Two image, it's already included.

Running a migration​

1. Build the two endpoints​

The full contract is in the User Migration API docs. A few things catch people out:

  • The username is percent-encoded in the path. frank@example.com arrives as frank%40example.com. Decode it before you look anything up, or every user returns a 404.
  • Any non-200 from the GET means "user not found", and any non-200 from the POST means "wrong password". A timeout or a rate limit looks the same as a bad password to the user, so log and alert on your error rate.
  • Secure the endpoints. They answer the question "is this the password?", so they are as sensitive as your login page. The provider supports bearer tokens and basic auth. Use HTTPS, and restrict access to Keycloak's egress IP addresses if you can.

If you are migrating from a hosted IdP rather than your own database, the POST usually calls that IdP's password grant or authentication API. Check that the IdP allows server-to-server calls at your login volume first. Our Azure AD B2C post explains why that check fails for B2C, and the Auth0 post shows a bridge that checks exported bcrypt hashes instead.

2. Add the provider to your realm​

In the admin console, go to User federation, choose User migration using a REST client, and enter your endpoint's base URL. The options you're most likely to set are:

  • Legacy role conversion and Group role conversion, to map legacy role and group names to Keycloak ones.
  • Update user on login (UPDATE_USER_ON_LOGIN), to refresh the profile from the legacy system while users are still linked to it.
  • Bearer token or basic auth credentials for your endpoints.

The full option list is in the upstream README.

3. Point your applications at Keycloak​

Users can only be migrated when they log in through Keycloak, so the migration starts when your applications switch to Keycloak for login. You can move applications one at a time. A user who logs in to the first migrated application is migrated for all of them.

4. Watch progress​

Compare the number of users in your Keycloak realm with the number of active users in your legacy system. The gap closes quickly at first, as your active users log in, and then flattens out. The flat part is your long tail: dormant accounts and people who log in rarely.

5. Finish the migration​

There's no need to wait for 100%. Once the curve has flattened, decide what to do with the remainder. Usually that means bulk-importing their profiles and setting the UPDATE_PASSWORD required action on each of them, so they choose a new password at their next login, or simply not migrating them.

Before you disable or delete the provider, unlink its users. Keycloak won't let a user log in while they're linked to a disabled provider, and deleting a provider deletes the users it imported. Open the provider in User federation and choose Unlink users from the Action menu. The details are in Turning the migration off.

Fast migration: moving everyone at once​

A fast migration is a bulk import. You export users from the legacy system, transform them into Keycloak's user format, and import them in one run. There's no bridge to keep running, and from the moment the import finishes every user exists in Keycloak, which matters if you need to assign roles, add users to organizations, or provision them to other systems before they ever log in.

What decides whether users notice is the password.

With password hashes​

If your legacy system can export password hashes in a format Keycloak can verify, you can import them and users keep their passwords. Keycloak verifies PBKDF2 (pbkdf2, pbkdf2-sha256, pbkdf2-sha512) and Argon2 hashes natively. Each user's credential carries the hash, the salt, and the parameters:

{
  "username": "frank@example.com",
  "email": "frank@example.com",
  "enabled": true,
  "emailVerified": true,
  "credentials": [
    {
      "type": "password",
      "secretData": "{\"value\":\"<base64 hash>\",\"salt\":\"<base64 salt>\"}",
      "credentialData": "{\"hashIterations\":27500,\"algorithm\":\"pbkdf2-sha256\"}"
    }
  ]
}

Import users in batches through the admin console's Partial import (under Realm settings > Action) or the POST /admin/realms/{realm}/partialImport endpoint. When a user logs in, Keycloak rehashes their password if it was stored with a different algorithm or iteration count than the realm's password policy asks for (Argon2 by default), so imported hashes are upgraded as users return.

Bcrypt, which many legacy systems and Auth0 use, isn't verified natively. You either add a custom password hash provider for it, which keeps bcrypt in your realm permanently, or validate bcrypt hashes in a slow-migration bridge, as in the Auth0 migration post.

Without password hashes​

If you can't export hashes (Okta and Azure AD B2C won't give them to you), a fast migration imports profiles only. Users then need a way in without their old password:

  • Set the UPDATE_PASSWORD required action on each user and send a reset email, so they choose a new password.
  • Let them in by magic link or email code instead of a password.
  • If they come from enterprise SSO or social login, configure the same identity providers in Keycloak. They have no password to migrate.

A mass reset email is the cost slow migration exists to avoid. Some users won't open it, and they will reach support instead.

Combining slow and fast migration​

Most real migrations use both, even with the user migration plugin installed. A slow migration on its own has no end date: the legacy system has to keep running until the last dormant user logs in, which might be never. Use a fast step to finish it:

  1. Run the slow migration first. Turn on the provider, switch your applications to Keycloak, and let your active users move over as they log in. Most of them do so in the first few weeks.
  2. Set a cutover date once the migrated count has flattened out. Tell users that accounts not used by then will need a new password.
  3. Bulk-import the rest. Export the users who haven't migrated and import them with a fast migration, using their hashes if you have them, or with UPDATE_PASSWORD set if you don't.
  4. Unlink the provider's users and turn the provider off, as described in Turning the migration off. Then shut down the legacy endpoints.

You can also run it the other way round: bulk-import profiles first, so every user exists in Keycloak with their roles and organizations, and keep the old system as an identity provider for logins until users have set a Keycloak password. Pick whichever order your legacy system makes easiest, but plan the fast step from the start, so that a slow migration has a finish line.

Choosing​

  • You can export hashes Keycloak verifies: fast migration. It's simpler, and nobody notices.
  • You can't export hashes, but the legacy system can check a password from a server: slow migration for active users, then a fast import of the tail at cutover.
  • The legacy system can only check passwords on its own login page: broker it as an identity provider while you move applications, then bulk-import profiles and have users set a new password.
  • Most users log in through social login or enterprise SSO: fast import of profiles, and configure the same identity providers in Keycloak.

On Phase Two​

The user migration provider is installed on every Phase Two cluster, so a slow migration only needs the two endpoints and the steps above, and a fast migration is a partial import through the admin console or API. See User Migration to get started, or contact us if you'd like help planning one.

item.title: Data residency requirements for SaaS authentication
item.description: The data residency requirements a DPO sends an authentication vendor, the document that answers each one, what a thin answer looks like, and ours filled in.
item.content:encoded:
Data residency requirements for a SaaS authentication service are not one requirement, they are four, and only the first of them is about a region. You have to name where each class of identity data is stored. You have to name a lawful transfer mechanism for every touchpoint outside that region, including remote administrative access, which is a transfer and not an exception to one. You have to hold Article 28 processing terms that say so in writing. And you have to be able to produce an inventory of where the identity data goes after it is stored — the brokers, mail relays, event listeners and relying parties your own realm sends it to. Below is the checklist a data protection officer sends, the document that answers each item, what a thin answer looks like, our own answers including the unflattering ones, and the commands that generate that fourth item from a running Keycloak realm, tested on 26.8.1.

Where the requirement actually comes from​

The single most useful thing to know before answering a residency questionnaire: the GDPR does not require data localisation. Chapter V regulates transfers out of the EEA, it does not mandate storage inside it. Almost every hard location requirement an authentication vendor is asked to meet comes from somewhere else — a sector rule, a national scheme, or a procurement framework — and those are the ones with teeth.

Where it comes fromWhat it says about locationWhat it asks you to produce
GDPR Chapter V (Art. 44–49)Nothing about storage location. Any transfer out of the EEA needs adequacy, an Art. 46 safeguard, or a derogationThe transfer mechanism per touchpoint, plus a transfer impact assessment where SCCs are used
GDPR Art. 28Nothing. Data location is a Chapter V disclosure, not an Art. 28 clauseA written processing agreement with the 28(3) content, a subprocessor list, notice and objection rights
DORA Art. 30(3) (financial entities, since 17 Jan 2025)Contract must state the locations where data is processed and stored, and notify changesQuantitative SLAs, audit and access rights, exit plan, subcontracting terms — and your entry in their Register of Information
NIS2 Art. 21(2)(d) and Art. 23Nothing about location; supply-chain security pushes the controls onto youAn incident notification window short enough to feed their 24-hour early warning and 72-hour notification
HDS v2 (French health data)Hosting in the EEA, and a published map of any extra-EEA transfer or accessCertification through the host, and the transfer map
BSI C5 (German public sector)Not a location rule, but jurisdiction, data location and subcontractors are explicit "Umfeldparameter"A C5 attestation or a credible mapping from ISO 27001
Commission Cloud Sovereignty Framework; the Cloud and AI Development Act proposal of 3 June 2026 (Art. 16)Location is one objective among eight, scored as a floor rather than an averageA scored self-assessment — see data residency vs data sovereignty for the SEAL levels

So "what are your data residency requirements" arriving from a procurement team is usually shorthand for a set of contract terms and evidence artifacts, of which the region field is the cheapest part. A vendor that answers only the region field has answered one row of seven.

The checklist, and the document that answers each item​

Ten items, in the order a DPO tends to send them. The middle column is the one worth internalising: every requirement here is satisfied by a document, and a vendor who can only answer in conversation cannot actually satisfy it.

What the DPO asks forThe artifact that answers itWhat a thin answer looks like
1. Where each class of identity data is stored — database, sessions, event store, backups, signing keys — and whether the region is fixed at creationA data map, one row per class, with the region and the infrastructure provider"Hosted in the EU" with no breakdown, or a region list that does not mention backups
2. Which of the vendor's own systems sit outside that region — dashboard, ticketing, billing, monitoring, loggingThe same data map, continued past the flattering rowsA map that stops at the Keycloak database
3. Whether staff outside the region can administer the serviceA statement that names it as a Chapter V restricted transfer, with the access controls"Support is EU-based" without saying where engineering and the control plane are
4. Which transfer mechanism covers each touchpoint outside the regionNamed instrument: an adequacy decision, or SCCs with the module, or a Data Privacy Framework certification number"We're GDPR compliant", or a DPF claim you cannot find in the US Commerce Department list
5. The transfer impact assessmentA written TIA covering FISA 702, EO 12333 and the CLOUD Act, with request history and challenge policy"Available under NDA" for a document that exists to be read by your DPO, or no TIA at all
6. Which legal entity is the counterparty, where it is incorporated, who owns it, and whether the parent is a subprocessorThe DPA's parties clause, plus a company registration number you can look upA trading name, a marketing entity, or a parent that appears nowhere in the agreement
7. The subprocessor list, with notice and an objection right before additionsA published, dated list naming the service each one performs (Art. 28(2) and 28(4))A list "available on request", or authorisation with no objection right
8. The breach notification window, in hoursThe DPA clause, stated numerically"Without undue delay", quoted back from Art. 33(2) as though it were a commitment
9. Audit and access rights, and whether DORA Art. 30(3) terms are acceptableSOC 2 Type II report, ISO 27001 certificate — and a written position on on-site auditCertifications offered in place of an answer about audit rights, or a flat refusal to negotiate
10. What an export contains and what deletion at end of service commits toAn export format, a worked example, and the Art. 28(3)(g) clauseAn "export" that turns out to be configuration without users, or deletion with no evidence of it

Three of those get fudged more than the rest.

Item 3 is the one most vendors skip, and it is the one most likely to come back during a supervisory authority review. Remote access to EU-stored data from a third country is itself a restricted transfer under Chapter V. A vendor whose engineers are distributed globally and whose control plane sits outside the EU is performing transfers every time someone opens a terminal, whether or not a byte of your database is ever copied abroad. The answer you want is not "no" — it is a precise description plus the safeguard.

Item 4 is where a residency claim either holds or does not. For a US touchpoint, the three available answers are an adequacy decision, SCCs plus a TIA, or a Data Privacy Framework certification. They are not equivalent, and the third is worth a sentence on its current state.

Item 5 is the one nobody can bluff. A TIA is six steps from EDPB Recommendations 01/2020: map the transfer, identify the tool, assess the destination country's law, add supplementary measures, formalise them, re-evaluate. It runs to pages and names statutes. A vendor who has one will send it; a vendor who has not will offer certifications instead.

Three facts behind items 4 and 5 that move, and that we re-verified on 26 October 2026. The EU–US Data Privacy Framework is in force; Philippe Latombe's appeal against the General Court's dismissal of his challenge is pending before the Court of Justice as Case C-703/25 P, with Microsoft admitted as an intervener by order of 4 June 2026 and no hearing announced. UK adequacy was renewed by the Commission on 19 December 2025 and runs to 27 December 2031, so an EU-to-UK transfer needs no additional safeguard today. And FISA Section 702's statutory authority lapsed in June 2026 when Congress did not reauthorise it, while collection continues under Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court certifications approved in March 2026 and running to 17 March 2027 — a lapsed statute over a live programme, which is why a TIA written in the last six months should not read as though the exposure went away.

The item you have to produce yourself: where does your realm send data?​

Items 1 to 10 are about the vendor. There is an eleventh that no questionnaire asks and every DPO eventually needs, because it is the controller's own answer rather than the processor's: where does identity data go once it is in the realm? Keycloak's own documentation has a Personal data collected by Keycloak section that enumerates what the server holds. It does not enumerate where the server sends it, and that is the part a transfer map needs.

Five outbound paths exist in a stock realm, and all five are readable from the Admin API. Everything below ran against Keycloak 26.8.1 on a realm with a brokered IdP and an SMTP relay configured:

docker run -d --name kc -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin \
  quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.1 start-dev

KC=http://127.0.0.1:8080
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST "$KC/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token" \
  -d client_id=admin-cli -d username=admin -d password=admin \
  -d grant_type=password | jq -r .access_token)
R=eu-demo
$ curl -s "$KC/admin/realms/$R/identity-provider/instances" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    | jq -r '.[] | "\(.alias)\t\(.providerId)\t\(.config.tokenUrl // .config.singleSignOnServiceUrl // "-")"'
corp-sso	oidc	https://login.corp-example.com/oauth2/v1/token

$ curl -s "$KC/admin/realms/$R/components?type=org.keycloak.storage.UserStorageProvider" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq -r 'length as $n | "user federation providers: \($n)"'
user federation providers: 0

$ curl -s "$KC/admin/realms/$R" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    | jq -r '.smtpServer | "\(.host // "-"):\(.port // "-")  from=\(.from // "-")"'
smtp.us-east-1.example.com:587  from=no-reply@example.de

$ curl -s "$KC/admin/realms/$R/events/config" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    | jq -c '{eventsListeners, eventsExpiration}'
{"eventsListeners":["jboss-logging"],"eventsExpiration":null}

$ curl -s "$KC/admin/realms/$R/clients" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    | jq -r '.[] | select(.redirectUris | length > 0) | "\(.clientId)\t\(.redirectUris | join(","))"'
account	/realms/eu-demo/account/*
account-console	/realms/eu-demo/account/*
portal	https://portal.example.de/*
security-admin-console	/admin/eu-demo/console/*

Read those five results as a transfer map. The brokered provider means authentication requests and returned claims traverse a third party — in this case one on a .com host whose region you have to look up rather than assume. The mail relay means every verification and reset email, each carrying an address and usually a name, leaves through whoever operates smtp.us-east-1.example.com; the hostname is a hint and not evidence, so check the contract behind it. The event listeners are where login records go, and "eventsExpiration": null means no retention is configured at all — the mechanics of fixing that on a realm that has run for a year without it are in user events in Keycloak and the audit log documentation, and a listener that ships events off-cluster is itself a transfer worth naming, which is what the webhooks documentation describes. The relying parties are recipients too, and the next section measures exactly what they receive.

One quirk to save you ten minutes: kcadm.sh get realms/eu-demo --fields smtpServer returns { } rather than the configuration, because the field filter does not descend into nested objects. Fetch the whole realm representation and filter client-side, as above.

Cut what leaves in the token​

A relying party is a recipient of personal data, and by default it receives more than most people assume. Here is the ID token a confidential client gets from a stock realm, decoded:

$ curl -s -X POST "$KC/realms/$R/protocol/openid-connect/token" \
    -d client_id=portal -d client_secret="$SECRET" -d grant_type=password \
    -d username=anja -d "password=$PW" -d scope=openid \
  | jq -r .id_token | cut -d. -f2 | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d | jq -S .
{
  "aud": "portal",
  "email": "anja@example.de",
  "email_verified": false,
  "family_name": "Keller",
  "given_name": "Anja",
  "name": "Anja Keller",
  "preferred_username": "anja",
  "sub": "07c581f0-db2f-4f0b-9c64-e83653fd61eb",
  ...
}

Email, full name and username, to every client, on every login, whether or not the application needs any of it. That comes from the profile and email client scopes, which are default scopes on every new client — meaning they apply whether or not the client asks. Move them from default to optional and the client gets them only when it requests them:

CID=$(curl -s "$KC/admin/realms/$R/clients?clientId=portal" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq -r '.[0].id')

for n in profile email; do
  SID=$(curl -s "$KC/admin/realms/$R/client-scopes" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    | jq -r --arg n "$n" '.[] | select(.name==$n) | .id')
  curl -s -X DELETE "$KC/admin/realms/$R/clients/$CID/default-client-scopes/$SID" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
  curl -s -X PUT "$KC/admin/realms/$R/clients/$CID/optional-client-scopes/$SID" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
done

The measured effect, same client, same credentials, two different scope values:

$ # scope=openid
["acr","at_hash","aud","azp","exp","iat","iss","jti","sid","sub","typ"]

$ # scope=openid profile email
["acr","at_hash","aud","azp","email","email_verified","exp","family_name","given_name",
 "iat","iss","jti","name","preferred_username","sid","sub","typ"]

Six personal-data claims gone from the default path, and the token still authenticates. The honest caveat: this breaks any application that reads email or name from the ID token without asking for the scope, which is a common shortcut — so audit what your clients request before you change the realm, and expect to fix a frontend or two. Moving the scopes to optional rather than deleting them is what keeps that fix a one-line change on the client side. What a token asserts and what signs it is in JWKS explained and the JWT tutorials.

Our answers, filled in​

Same ten items, our side of them, including the rows we would rather not write.

#Phase Two
1EU clusters: database, sessions, event store and realm signing keys in Frankfurt (eu-central-1), backups in Ireland (eu-west-1), never replicated outside the EU. A cluster's region is fixed at creation. Full list in the regions documentation
2Dashboard account metadata, support tickets and billing run in the United States. That is our business systems, not your end users' identity data, and it is in the data map rather than omitted from it
3Yes. Our control plane runs in the US and our engineering team is distributed globally, so administrative access to an EU cluster can come from outside the EU. We disclose it as a Chapter V restricted transfer; access is limited to named operations roles and logged internally
4EU to UK: the Commission's adequacy decision of 19 December 2025. US administrative access: Standard Contractual Clauses, Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, incorporated into the DPA. We are not certified under the Data Privacy Framework and do not rely on it
5A transfer impact assessment exists and we share it on request, without an NDA
6Phase Two UK, Ltd, registered in England and Wales, company number 16815578, 2 Leman Street, London E1W 9US. Parent: Phase Two, Inc., Seattle, United States, which acts as a subprocessor to the UK entity and is named as such in the agreement
7Published in the Trust Center with the service each one performs. Notice before adding or replacing one, and an objection right
872 hours. Read that against your own clock: NIS2 gives you 24 hours for an early warning, so raise it during contracting rather than during an incident
9SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001, both current. DORA Art. 30(3) audit and access rights are negotiated rather than refused
10Realm configuration and users export through the Admin API and kc.sh export; a database dump on request. Deletion at end of service under Art. 28(3)(g), carried out on request. We do not yet issue a certificate of deletion — if your risk assessment needs one, ask and it goes in the contract

The whole data map, class by class, is in where your Keycloak data lives, and the Article 28 terms behind rows 4 through 10 are on the data processing agreement page.

What we do not claim​

  • We do not describe ourselves as sovereign. Our parent is US-incorporated, so we cannot claim immunity from US legal process, and we would read any vendor that does claim it carefully. What we do with a legal demand is on the government requests page; the count received to date is zero.
  • We will not hold SecNumCloud qualification — it requires European ownership a US-parented company cannot satisfy — and we hold no BSI C5 attestation of our own.
  • Realm signing keys for EU clusters are held in our key management service in the Frankfurt region. They are our keys in our KMS; we do not offer bring-your-own-key on hosted clusters today.
  • Administrative access logs are examined in our SOC 2 Type II audit but are not exposed to customers. We would like to change that.
  • Support is in English only.

Where to start​

Run the five Admin API calls above against your own realm first. The result is the one artifact in this whole checklist that no vendor can produce for you, it takes about a minute, and in our experience it is where the surprise is — an SMTP relay or an event listener nobody wrote down beats a region field nobody checked.

If you are evaluating us against that list, the complete map, the subprocessor list and the questions our own DPO gets most are on the EU data residency page, and the terms behind them are on the data processing agreement page.

Keycloak behaviour in this post was tested on 26.8.1 against the 26.8.1 Server Administration Guide. Regulatory facts were verified on 26 October 2026: UK adequacy against the Commission's December 2025 renewal; the status of Case C-703/25 P against current legal reporting, which has the appeal pending with no hearing announced and Microsoft admitted as an intervener by order of 4 June 2026; and the status of FISA Section 702 against reporting from June 2026 onward and the Brennan Center's explainer as updated on 16 October 2026, with nothing enacted since. DORA Art. 30(3), GDPR Art. 28 and Chapter V, and EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 were read in their published texts.

item.title: What Azure AD B2C's end of sale actually means
item.description: Azure AD B2C is end of sale, not end of life — supported to at least May 2030. What the March 2026 P2 date really was, and the three destinations worth considering.
item.content:encoded:
Azure AD B2C's end of sale means Microsoft stopped selling it to new customers on 1 May 2025 and committed to supporting it until at least May 2030. It is not being shut down. Existing customers keep their tenants, can still create new ones, and keep the SLA, the security updates and the compliance posture. What ended is the roadmap.

One other date is doing a lot of damage. Premium P2 was discontinued on 15 March 2026 for all customers, and tenants moved to P1. That is a pricing-tier retirement, not a tenant retirement — but it has been reported often enough as "B2C shuts down in March 2026" that it is worth saying plainly: your tenant is fine, and you have roughly four years to make a decision rather than four months to execute one.

Four years is enough time to make a good decision and short enough that the one you make now is the one you live with. Here is what the three realistic destinations actually cost.

The dates, and nothing else​

Every date below is from Microsoft's own B2C FAQ. There are only three.

DateWhat changedWhat did not change
1 May 2025B2C is no longer available to purchase for new customersExisting customers keep using it, and can still create tenants — on P1
15 March 2026Premium P2 discontinued for all customers; tenants switched to P1Everything that is not a P2-only feature
May 2030The earliest date the support commitment runs toSLAs, security updates and compliance, all unchanged until then

Microsoft's wording on the last one is "We'll continue supporting Azure AD B2C until at least May 2030." At least is doing real work there — it is a floor, not an expiry.

The P2 retirement is the one worth understanding properly, because it is the only one that took a capability away from a running tenant. Microsoft's FAQ describes it as a separate matter from the end of sale: P2 is retired in B2C tenants, P2-only features go with it, ID Protection among them, and the guidance for teams that depended on it is to integrate a third-party identity verification provider. Workforce tenants are unaffected.

So the accurate summary of your position is: end of sale, frozen roadmap, legacy status, one tier of capability removed, supported for about four more years. Nothing in that sentence is an emergency, and nothing in it is good news either.

What "frozen roadmap" costs you, slowly​

A product under support but not under development degrades in ways that do not show up on a status page.

The features you do not get are the ones the rest of the industry ships in the meantime. Between now and 2030, standards move — the places where that usually bites a customer identity deployment are new authentication methods, new token-binding and sender-constraint mechanisms, and whatever the regulatory environment demands next. B2C will get security fixes for what it has. It will not get capability it does not have.

The second cost is the one teams underestimate: the pool of people who know the product stops growing. Identity Experience Framework expertise was never abundant. On a product nobody new can buy, it thins out. If your custom policies are maintained by one person, their next job offer is a platform risk.

Neither of those is a reason to move this quarter. Both are reasons not to let the decision drift to 2029.

Why "B2C retires in March 2026" spread​

Because two announcements landed close together and one of them had a hard date on it.

The end of sale is open-ended — "at least May 2030" is not a deadline anyone can build a headline around. The P2 discontinuation is a specific day, applies to every customer, and genuinely removes something. Compress those and you get "Microsoft is killing B2C in March 2026", which is wrong in the one direction that causes bad decisions: it makes a four-year planning problem look like a four-month migration.

If you are being pushed toward a rushed migration on the strength of that date, check the FAQ. The person pushing is either misinformed or selling.

Option 1: stay on B2C until 2030​

This is the right answer for more teams than vendor blogs admit, and it deserves to be stated without qualification: if B2C is working for you, staying is a defensible engineering decision.

It fits when most of these are true:

  • Your authentication is built on built-in user flows, not custom policies.
  • You are inside the 50,000 free monthly active users tier, or comfortably near it.
  • Your stack is Azure-native and you use what that gives you — Front Door custom domains, Application Insights, federation to your Entra workforce tenant.
  • Nobody is asking you about data residency, source access, or what happens to identity if the vendor relationship changes.
  • You did not depend on a P2-only feature.

What you are buying is zero operational burden and a Microsoft SLA, which are worth a great deal and which no self-hosted alternative gives you for free. What you are deferring is a decision, not avoiding it. Put a review in the calendar for 2028 and move on to something that matters more this year.

Option 2: move to Microsoft Entra External ID​

External ID is Microsoft's named successor and has been generally available since 2024. For a simple B2C tenant it is the path of least resistance: same vendor, same portal, same Graph API, same invoice.

The caveats are not hidden — they are in Microsoft's own migration guide, which is the document to read before anything else. Its feature-mapping table is the honest part of the whole discussion:

B2CExternal ID equivalent
Custom policies (XML/IEF)Custom authentication extensions
Hosted pages with HTML/CSSUser flows with branding + native authentication
Custom policies, user flow conditionsMicrosoft Entra conditional access
Custom claims in policiesCustom authentication extensions
Browser-based flows, web redirectsNative authentication SDKs (local accounts only)

Read the left column as "what you have" and the right as "what you will build instead". These are mappings between concepts, not a migration path for artifacts. There is no converter that takes TrustFrameworkExtensions.xml and emits the equivalent.

The guide is also explicit about one gap that catches enterprise tenants:

Social identity providers configured through B2C custom policies. Social federation must be reconfigured using External ID's built-in social identity provider support. Third-party identity providers configured through B2C custom policies aren't supported.

If you federate to a partner's IdP, a regional identity scheme, or anything you wired up yourself through a custom policy, that is the sentence that decides your project. Check it first, before you cost anything else.

Two smaller things worth knowing: native authentication — the SDK path that avoids a browser redirect on mobile — is documented as local-accounts only, and User Insights is being retired on 31 August 2026 in favour of Azure Monitor with Log Analytics.

None of this makes External ID a bad product. It makes it a new product, and Microsoft's own positioning leans toward new deployments rather than B2C lift-and-shift.

Option 3: move to Keycloak​

Here is the argument, and it only works if you accept the two paragraphs above.

If your B2C tenant is built on custom policies, you are rewriting your authentication logic whichever destination you choose. That is not a Keycloak talking point; it follows from Microsoft's own feature-mapping table. Once the rewrite is a fixed cost on every option, the question changes from "which migration is cheapest?" to "where do I want to be standing the next time a vendor freezes a roadmap?"

That is the whole case. It is not urgency and it is not cost.

Concretely, what Keycloak gives a B2C tenant:

  • Authentication flows that behave like user journeys. Executions in order, subflows with conditions, requirement levels per step. Most orchestration steps become configuration rather than XML — see building a custom authentication flow.
  • The Authenticator SPI for the parts that genuinely need code, which is a normal Java interface in your own build pipeline rather than a policy language.
  • Full theme control — login, account, email and admin — so the HTML/CSS customization you have in B2C's hosted pages does not narrow to a branding menu. Keycloak themes.
  • Any OIDC or SAML identity provider, plus LDAP and Active Directory federation, without a supported-list gate.
  • Your own database, which means your credentials are portable the next time this question comes up.
  • Deployment anywhere — your cloud, on-premise, Kubernetes — which is how a residency requirement gets answered rather than negotiated.

And the honest other side. Keycloak is a JVM application with a database, a cache, a certificate story and a quarterly release cadence, and only the latest minor gets community patches — 26.8 at the time of writing, released 1 October 2026. Running it well is a real job. Either you staff it or you buy managed Keycloak; pretending it is free is how migrations go wrong.

The four questions that decide this​

Answer these before you cost anything.

  1. How much of your logic is in custom policies? Open the Azure portal, go to Identity Experience Framework, and count the policy files and the orchestration steps. Zero means all three options are cheap. A TrustFrameworkExtensions.xml with ten orchestration steps and REST calls means one expensive rebuild, on any destination.
  2. Do you federate to anything outside the built-in social providers? If yes, read Microsoft's unsupported-features note again and establish whether External ID can do it at all before you treat it as the default.
  3. Does anyone need identity to run somewhere specific? A customer contract, a regulator, a data protection impact assessment. If yes, a single-cloud product is a structural problem and no amount of feature parity fixes it.
  4. What is your MAU trajectory? Inside 50,000, B2C is free and cost is not an argument for anything. Well past it, the per-MAU line is worth modelling against fixed infrastructure cost — but model it, do not assume it.

If the answers are "none, no, no, under 50k", stay on B2C. That is a real recommendation and we will put it in writing.

Do this next​

Spend an afternoon producing one artifact: an inventory of your tenant. User flows, custom policy files and their orchestration steps, every identity provider and how it was configured, every custom claim, and your current MAU. That document is the input to all three options and it is the thing nobody has when they ask for an estimate.

For the technical half, porting Azure AD B2C custom policies to Keycloak maps the Identity Experience Framework concept by concept and is explicit about what has no equivalent.

The side-by-side is on Keycloak vs. Azure AD B2C, and if you want someone who has done this to read your inventory and tell you what it costs, talk to us about migrating to Keycloak. If the answer is "stay until 2028", we will tell you that too.

item.title: Which Keycloak clients should be enabled when you go live?
item.description: Automated scanners probe every default Keycloak client the day your realm goes public. Which clients and grant types to leave on, which to turn off, and why disabling clients is mostly the wrong lever. Measured on Keycloak 26.8.1.
item.content:encoded:
The day a Keycloak realm is reachable from the internet, automated scanners find it. They read /realms/<name>/.well-known/openid-configuration, try every client ID that ships with every realm against the token endpoint and the login pages, and start replaying username and password pairs leaked from other sites. The traffic arrives from a different residential IP on almost every request, so it looks nothing like one noisy attacker. What you are trying to stop is not a single brute-force run. It is account takeover through credential stuffing, plus the enumeration that tells an attacker which of your users exist.

So the go-live question is not "should I disable admin-cli?" It is "which clients, and which grant types, should be on at all?" The short answer: the password grant off on every client, enforced by policy; only the clients you actually use exposed; a CAPTCHA on every flow that renders a login page; and account left enabled. Disabling a client is one tool among several, and for account it is usually the wrong one.

Everything below was reproduced against Keycloak 26.8.1, and every error string is copied out of a real response.

What the probe sees​

This is the first request a scanner sends: POST /realms/prod/protocol/openid-connect/token with grant_type=password, client_id=admin-cli and a wrong password. Here is what it gets back from four states of the same realm:

Realm stateStatus and errorWhat the attacker learns
Defaults400 invalid_grant: "Invalid user credentials"Password grant is live. Start the dictionary.
Direct Access Grants off on admin-cli400 unauthorized_client: "Client not allowed for direct access grants"Client exists, door shut. Try the other five IDs.
admin-cli disabled401 invalid_client: "Invalid client or Invalid client credentials"Same answer as a client that never existed.
Client policy rejecting the grant400 invalid_grant: "resource owner password credentials grant is prohibited."No client here takes a password. Move on.

The full body of the default response, for reference:

{"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"Invalid user credentials"}

A wrong password and an unknown username return the same body, so usernames do not leak. Which clients exist, and which accept passwords, does.

admin-cli: the grant is the problem, not the client​

Out of the box, admin-cli is the only built-in client with the password grant on:

ClientPublicDirect Access GrantsFull scope allowed
admin-cliyesonon
security-admin-consoleyesoffon
account, account-consoleyesoffoff
realm-management, brokerbearer-onlyoffoff

It bypasses your browser flow. The default direct grant flow is username, password, then a conditional OTP step that only fires for users with a TOTP device. Side by side with the browser flow on the same server:

direct grant                       browser (forms subflow)
  Username Validation  REQUIRED      Username Password Form     REQUIRED
  Password             REQUIRED      Browser - Conditional 2FA  CONDITIONAL
  Conditional OTP      CONDITIONAL     Condition - credential   REQUIRED
    OTP                REQUIRED        OTP Form                 ALTERNATIVE
                                       WebAuthn Authenticator   DISABLED
                                       Recovery Codes           DISABLED

No WebAuthn, no passkeys, no CAPTCHA, none of the steps you added to the browser flow. A passkey-only user gets a token for a password alone. RFC 9700, the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, says the password grant "MUST NOT be used" and "is not designed to work with two-factor authentication".

It is the cleaner target for credential stuffing. Brute force detection does cover the token endpoint, but it is per user. A spray of one guess per username per window, from a rotating pool of residential IPs, slides under per-user lockout and under per-IP limits at the proxy at the same time. Edge rate limiting is worth having; it is not what stops this.

Disabling it does not shrink the Admin API. Admin requests are authorized from the roles of the user behind the token, filtered by what the client may scope. A realm admin's admin-cli token carries no roles at all (it is a lightweight token) and still gets 200 from /admin/realms/prod/users. The same user through an application client with Full scope allowed on gets the same 200, now with every realm-management role visible in resource_access. With Full scope allowed off on that client, the call returns 403, and 26.8.1 logs a warning for every token issued with the switch on:

WARN  [org.keycloak.protocol.oidc.endpoints.TokenEndpoint.full-scope-allowed] Client 'webapp' in the realm
'prod' has 'Full scope allowed' switch enabled. This client switch is deprecated and will be removed in the
future. Please update your client settings to disable the switch and configure needed roles, which this
client application needs, to the client role scope

So the hardening is per realm:

  • Reject the password grant with a client policy. A client profile with the reject-ropc-grant executor, Auto-configure on, bound to a policy with the any-client condition. Every client then answers resource owner password credentials grant is prohibited., and any client created or updated afterwards has Direct Access Grants switched off for you. Set Auto-configure explicitly: left unset, client creation fails with a null pointer on 26.8.1. The same executor ships inside the built-in oauth-2-1-for-public-client and oauth-2-1-for-confidential-client profiles.
  • Automation uses service accounts. A confidential client, client_credentials only, with the specific realm-management roles it needs. A provisioner client holding only manage-users lists users with 200 and is refused on /clients with 403, which is the shape a user-sync job should have. realm-admin belongs to people behind MFA, not to a secret in a pipeline.
  • Full scope allowed off on every application client, enforced with the full-scope-disabled executor if you have many.
  • Non-master realms: disable admin-cli once nothing runs kcadm against them. In master, keep it only while tooling depends on it and restrict /admin/* and /realms/master/* at the edge. On a Phase Two cluster, admin-path IP restrictions do this and master is not exposed to customers.

account and account-console: remove the roles, not the client​

account is not a login surface. It is the audience and role container for the Account REST API: /realms/prod/account/ accepts a token that carries manage-account or view-profile under resource_access.account, and users get those roles through default-roles-<realm>.

Disabling it does work as a kill switch; console and API both return 404 {"error":"account management not enabled"}. It also has a side effect that changed in Keycloak 26. execute-actions-email and send-verify-email called without a client_id used to fail with 400 Client is not enabled. Since 26.0.0 Keycloak creates a confidential client named _system on the fly and issues the email link against it:

WARN  [org.keycloak.models.utils.SystemClientUtil] Client 'account' not available. Creating system client
'_system' for system operations

The reset email still arrives, and the next audit finds a client nobody created. If the goal is no self-service through Keycloak:

  • Disable account-console, the PKCE public client behind the UI, or bind a Deny-access flow override to it as Account Console describes.
  • Remove manage-account and manage-account-links from default-roles-<realm>. Measured: reads of /account/ still return 200 through view-profile, writes return 403. Remove view-profile too and the token loses the account audience entirely, so every call returns 401.

If you keep self-service, the residual risk is a hijacked session changing credentials. Require re-authentication for credential changes with kc_action and max_age, keep SSO idle short, and require the current password on password change.

security-admin-console, realm-management, broker​

security-admin-console is a bigger surface than either client above: in a non-master realm it is the realm-scoped admin UI at /admin/<realm>/console/, public, PKCE, Full scope allowed on. If no realm-scoped administrator uses it, disable it; the login redirect then renders Keycloak's Client disabled. page. Otherwise keep it and block the path at the edge. On a Phase Two cluster, keep it enabled: the dashboard's Console link signs in through it. Restrict /admin/* with IP restrictions instead.

realm-management and broker are bearer-only role containers. There is no flow to attack, and the admin roles and the broker read-token role hang off them. Leave them alone.

Rate limiting is not enough: put a CAPTCHA in the flow​

Per-IP limits assume the attacker has an IP. Per-user lockout assumes they want one user. Credential stuffing today has neither property, which is why a CAPTCHA earns its place: it taxes the automation, not the address. Keycloak's built-in reCAPTCHA only covers registration, so for login you need an extension. The Cloudflare Turnstile integration in our open-source keycloak-magic-link extension is the one we recommend. It is included in every Phase Two cluster and stays off until you add your own Cloudflare keys and place it in your flows; Cloudflare Turnstile walks through it. It is three authenticators sharing one configuration (site key, secret, action), which is what makes it a flow edit rather than a project:

  • Cloudflare Turnstile Username Password Form replaces the stock login form with the widget embedded in the page. Unconfigured, it behaves exactly like the original. On its own it does not block anything: it checks the challenge after the password is accepted and only records a failure on the session, so a scripted login with a valid password still gets tokens. Pair it with one of the next two steps. Its Verify email on CAPTCHA failure option is the other way to make it block: a failed challenge stops the login at email verification, at the cost of marking the account's email as unverified, real users included.
  • Condition - Turnstile Failed gates a 2FA subflow on the CAPTCHA result: Required means only sessions that failed the challenge are asked for a second factor, Disabled means 2FA for everyone with a factor enrolled. Adaptive friction from one requirement toggle. Use a factor every user already has, such as email OTP. With an OTP Form step, a user who has no authenticator yet is sent to set one up, so an attacker holding the password enrolls their own.
  • Cloudflare Turnstile validation is a standalone challenge page. Placed before the login form, it refuses a submission without a valid token outright, which is the simplest way to stop scripted logins. Place it before any step that sends email too, such as magic link or email OTP, so bots cannot turn your SMTP relay into a flood.
  • The registration form action validates the challenge on sign-up, so bulk account creation, and the abusive takeovers that follow it, stop.

Setup is two settings: https://challenges.cloudflare.com in frame-src under Security Defenses, and the cloudflare-turnstile login theme on the realm or one client. No image puzzles, which matters when the people solving it are your customers.

This closes the loop with the first section. A CAPTCHA protects flows that render a page. The token endpoint renders nothing, so with the password grant enabled an attacker simply takes the path without one. The two controls only work together.

Go-live defaults for every client​

This is what each client should look like on the day you launch. The rest of the launch list is in the go-live checklist.

ClientDefaultProduction
admin-clipublic, password grant on, full scope onPassword grant off, policy-enforced. Disable in non-master realms once nothing uses it.
security-admin-consolepublic, PKCE, full scope onDisable where no realm-scoped admins exist, or block /admin/* at the edge. On Phase Two, keep it and use IP restrictions.
accountpublic, role container, API audienceKeep enabled. Remove manage-account and manage-account-links from default roles if self-service is unwanted.
account-consolepublic, PKCEDisable or deny-flow when self-service is unwanted.
realm-management, brokerbearer-onlyLeave alone.
Your application clientswhatever you clickedPassword grant off, full scope off, PKCE, Turnstile on login and registration, placed so a failed challenge blocks.

All of this fits in a realm export you keep in version control. If you would rather start from a realm configured this way, Phase Two runs managed Keycloak with Turnstile, magic links and admin-path restrictions included, and a 30-day Starter trial from $149/month. Self-hosting is the right call for plenty of teams: the production readiness checklist covers the server-side settings next to these, brute force detection covers the per-user side, and the WAF question covers what belongs at the edge. The go-live checklist is where it all lands before launch.

item.title: Passkeys make login faster. Here is the data, and how to roll them out in Keycloak
item.description: Google, Microsoft and the FIDO Alliance all measured passkey sign-in against passwords. Passkeys came out two to three times faster and far more reliable. What the numbers say, why it happens, and how to introduce passkeys in Keycloak without forcing anyone.
item.content:encoded:
Every second a customer spends on your login page is a second they might spend somewhere else. Typing an email and password, mistyping it, waiting for a code, switching to an authenticator app, or giving up and resetting the password are all time between someone deciding to sign in and actually getting in. Passkeys remove most of those steps, and every large published measurement shows the same result: sign-in with a passkey takes about half the time, or less, and fails far less often. Our own customers report the same: after introducing passkeys, they measured login times drop by several seconds per sign-in.

This post collects the published figures, explains where the time goes, and shows how to introduce passkeys in Keycloak alongside the password login you already have.

What the published numbers say​

Three organizations with very large sign-in volumes have published measurements comparing passkeys with passwords. They measured different things in different ways, so the figures are not interchangeable, but they all point in the same direction.

SourceSign-in timeSign-in success
Google, March–April 2023 data14.9 seconds with a passkey, 30.4 seconds with a password63.8% for same-device passkeys, 13.8% for passwords
Microsoft, December 20243x faster than a password, 8x faster than a password plus traditional MFA98% with a passkey, 32% with a password
FIDO Alliance Passkey Index, October 20258.5 seconds with a passkey, 31.2 seconds with traditional MFA, a 73% decrease93% with a passkey, 63% with other methods

The FIDO Alliance figures are worth a closer look if you run a store. They come from a survey of nine organizations that have run passkeys for one to three years, including Amazon, Target, PayPal and Mercari, so this is not a lab result. The same report notes up to an 81% reduction in sign-in-related help desk incidents. Microsoft adds a figure that matters for rollout: 99% of users who start passkey registration finish it.

"Success rate" deserves a word. These are the share of sign-in attempts that end with the user signed in. A password attempt that fails because of a typo, a forgotten password, or an abandoned reset counts as a failure. That is why the gap is so wide. Passkeys do not just save seconds on the happy path; they cut out the unhappy paths that cost the most time of all.

Where the time goes​

A password sign-in has more steps than it looks like:

  1. Type or autofill the email address.
  2. Type or autofill the password, or fail to remember it.
  3. If MFA is on, wait for an SMS or email code, or open an authenticator app, and type six digits.
  4. On any mistake, start again, and after a few mistakes, reset the password by email.

A passkey sign-in is one step after the email address, and often not even that. The browser offers the passkey in the username field's autofill, the user confirms with a fingerprint, face, or device PIN, and they are in. There is nothing to type, nothing to remember, and no code to wait for. Because a passkey is already a possession factor confirmed with a biometric or PIN, it replaces the password and the second factor at once, which is why the gap against "password plus MFA" is so much larger than against a password alone.

Faster and harder to steal​

The speed is the easy sell. The security benefit is the one that compounds. A passkey is a key pair: the private key never leaves the user's device and is bound to your domain. There is no shared secret on your side to leak, nothing a phishing page can collect, and nothing an attacker can replay from another site's breach.

That last point is what matters for credential stuffing, the automated replay of leaked passwords that every public login page faces. A customer who signs in with a passkey has nothing for that attack to guess. Keep in mind that as long as the password path stays open for an account, an attacker can still try it, so passkeys reduce your exposure as adoption grows rather than eliminating it on day one. The rest of the defenses still matter: see Credential Stuffing and Account Takeover.

Will your customers understand it?​

Most of them already know more than you might expect. In the FIDO Alliance's 2025 consumer survey of 1,389 adults across five countries, 74% had heard of passkeys and 69% had turned them on for at least one account. About half already considered them more secure (53%) or more convenient (54%) than passwords.

The word itself is the hard part. Microsoft found that "passkey" was often unfamiliar, but "face, fingerprint, or PIN" was well understood, so its screens connect the two. It also tested how to pitch them: a message about faster sign-in drew 27% click-through and one about security 24%, while "easier" did noticeably worse. And customers enroll when you ask them, not on their own: about a quarter of the people who saw Microsoft's prompt engaged with it, while enrollment from account settings was under 1% of the total.

That plays out differently depending on who your customer is:

  • The customer who has never heard the word. Think of the least technical person who buys from you. They have never set up a passkey on purpose, but they unlock their phone with their face or fingerprint every day. Show them "Sign in with your face, fingerprint, or screen lock," not "Create a passkey." Keep their password and email recovery working so they are never stuck, and never make the passkey a condition of signing in.
  • The average customer. They have probably already been offered a passkey by Google, Apple, or a large retailer, and may have accepted. Ask once, right after a successful sign-in, and lead with speed, the message that tested best. If they decline, do not ask again on every visit.
  • The technical customer. They want control. They will register more than one passkey, keep them in a password manager, or use a hardware security key, and they will look for a place to see and remove their passkeys. Keycloak's Account Console covers that, and this is the one group for whom settings-based enrollment works.

Across all three, the pattern is the same: a plain-language prompt at the right moment does more than any amount of availability in a settings page.

Introducing passkeys in Keycloak​

On Keycloak 26.7 and later, passwordless passkeys are a realm setting rather than a flow you build. Realm settings → Login → Enable Passkeys turns them on for the stock browser flow, which then offers a passkey option and tags the username field for browser autofill. Users who have not registered a passkey sign in exactly as before.

The rollout that works is gradual:

  1. Turn on passkeys without removing passwords. Existing customers keep signing in the way they know, and passkeys appear as an option.
  2. Prompt enrollment right after sign-in, not at a gate. Microsoft invites users to enroll immediately after they authenticate, and nearly everyone who starts registration finishes it. Do not put registration between a customer and their checkout. In Keycloak, do this as an application-initiated action: after sign-in, show your own short prompt, and if the customer says yes, send them to the authorization endpoint with kc_action=webauthn-register-passwordless. Keycloak shows the registration page with a cancel option and reports the outcome back to your application in kc_action_status. Avoid setting Webauthn Register Passwordless as a required action on users instead: a required action has to be completed before the user can continue, which is exactly the gate to avoid. The Account Console lets users add and remove passkeys themselves, but expect few to find it unprompted.
  3. Leave the default mediation alone. The default, conditional mediation, offers passkeys through the browser's autofill without an extra dialog, which is the fastest experience for users who have one and invisible to users who do not.
  4. Measure before and after. Record time from the login page loading to the user landing back in your application, and the share of sign-in attempts that succeed, split by method. Those are the two numbers every published study uses, and they are the ones your own customers will feel.

The full setup, including passkeys as a second factor instead of a replacement and the ways each setup can fail quietly, is in Passkeys and WebAuthn in Keycloak. If you want to know which credential type you actually want, start with Keycloak passkeys and WebAuthn: what's the difference?. The Passkeys docs cover the Phase Two specifics.

When a passkey doesn't work​

Passkeys are supported in every current major browser and operating system, but "supported" is not "works every time for every customer." Plan for the attempts that fail, because a customer who cannot get in will not wait for you to fix it. The common causes:

  • An older browser or operating system that does not support passkeys, or a managed work device where they are turned off by policy.
  • An in-app browser. A customer who taps your link inside a social or messaging app often lands in that app's embedded browser, which may not support passkeys at all. Your own mobile app has the same problem if it shows login in an embedded web view; use the system browser for sign-in instead, which is the recommended practice for OAuth in native apps anyway.
  • The passkey is on a different device. A passkey saved to a phone is not automatically on the customer's work laptop. Signing in with a phone by scanning a QR code works, but it needs Bluetooth on both devices and the phone nearby.
  • The passkey was deleted from the device or password manager, while Keycloak still has it registered.
  • The customer cancels the prompt, or the fingerprint or face check fails. The browser reports a timeout, a cancellation and a refusal as the same generic error, so your login page cannot tell them apart. Treat them all as "offer another way."

None of these should end in a dead end. The fallback design that works:

  1. Keep the password on the same page. Keycloak's Enable Passkeys setting already does this. The login page keeps the username and password fields and adds the passkey option next to them. If the browser can't offer a passkey, or the customer dismisses the autofill, nothing visible happens and the password field works as usual. If they click Sign in with Passkey and the passkey fails or they cancel, the login page comes back with a short "try again" message and the password field still there. Passkeys has the details.
  2. Offer a passwordless fallback if you have dropped passwords. In a flow where the passkey is one of several alternative steps, Keycloak shows a Try another way link that lets the customer pick a different method. A magic link or an email one-time code is the natural choice, because every customer has an inbox and nothing to remember.
  3. Say it in plain language. "Use your password instead" or "Email me a sign-in link" next to the passkey button, not an error code. The customer who never wanted a passkey should not have to understand why it failed. In Keycloak you can relabel the passkey button itself, for example to "Sign in with face, fingerprint, or screen lock," with a realm localization override; Passkeys shows how.
  4. Keep recovery independent of the passkey. Forgot password or an emailed link must work for a customer who has lost every device. Never make the passkey the only way back into an account. Encourage customers to use passkeys that sync across their devices, so one lost phone is not a lost account.
  5. Measure the fallback rate. Track how often a passkey attempt ends with the customer signing in another way, by browser and platform. A rising rate on one platform is usually an in-app browser or an operating system update, and it is much cheaper to find in a dashboard than in support tickets.

Treat the passkey as the fast path, not the only path. The speed gains in the published numbers come from the customers for whom it works, and the fallback is what keeps the rest from abandoning.

What to watch for​

  • Direct grant. Passkeys only work in browser flows. A client with Direct Access Grants enabled accepts a password at the token endpoint with no passkey step at all. Turn it off; see Sign-in Methods, Grant Types and Clients.

Do this next​

Turn on passkeys in a non-production realm, register one, and time a sign-in with it against a sign-in with a password and your current second factor. Then put the same two numbers on a dashboard for production before you enable it there, so you can show the difference.

If you run Keycloak with Phase Two, passkeys are available on every cluster and need no extension or custom flow. The go-live checklist covers the rest of what to check before launch.

item.title: Replacing homegrown e-commerce login with Keycloak
item.description: How an e-commerce store replaces homegrown login with Keycloak, migrates customers without password resets, and defends the login page against credential stuffing.
item.content:encoded:
The login page is the most attacked page on an online store, and it is rarely the one anyone designed for attack. Homegrown e-commerce login usually starts as a users table, a bcrypt column and a session cookie, and it grows a password reset, a mobile API, a trade-account flag and a social button over the years. What it almost never grows is a defense against credential stuffing: automated replay of email and password pairs leaked from other sites, aimed at whichever of your customers reused one. Replacing homegrown login with Keycloak gives a store one identity service for web, app and back office, with social login, B2B accounts and branded pages built in, and you can move customers onto it without asking anyone to reset a password. It does not make the login page safe on its own. The defaults leave doors open that attackers look for first, and the rest of this post covers both halves: what you gain, and what has to be layered on top.

Why does homegrown store login fall behind?​

The trouble is rarely the password hashing. Most homegrown systems hash correctly. It is everything around the hash:

NeedTypical homegrown loginKeycloak
Social login (Google, Apple, Facebook)One provider, bolted on, often a separate account per providerIdentity providers configured per realm, with linking to an existing account by email
Web, mobile app and back-office servicesSeparate session logic per surface, often a shared API key for servicesOne OpenID Connect issuer; browser, app and service clients each get the grant they need
B2B or trade customersA flag on the user row, pricing logic scattered through the appOrganizations with members, roles and per-company identity providers
Two-factor and passkeysUsually absentOTP, WebAuthn and passkeys as flow steps
Branded login and emailHand-built templatesKeycloak themes for login, account and email pages
Audit trail of loginsApplication logs, if anyone added themLogin and admin events with IP, client and error
Bot and credential-stuffing defenseRarely more than a per-IP limitBrute force detection built in, CAPTCHA by extension; still needs configuration (below)

The last row is the one that matters most, and it is the one Keycloak does not solve by being installed.

What does a store get from Keycloak?​

One login for every surface. The storefront, the mobile app, the customer-service tool and the order API all trust the same issuer. A customer who signs in on the app is the same subject in your order system, and your backend services authenticate as themselves through service accounts instead of borrowing a human's password.

Social login that does not fork the customer. When someone who registered with an email address later taps "Continue with Google", Keycloak recognizes the matching email and offers to link the Google identity to the existing account once the customer proves they own it, rather than creating a second one. See Social Login.

Trade accounts as a first-class object. Stores that sell to both consumers and businesses usually end up with a business flag on the user and a lot of conditional code. Organizations model the company itself: its members, their roles inside it, and optionally the company's own SSO. A buyer at a contractor firm signs in through their employer's identity provider and lands in the right account. The multi-tenancy post walks through the model.

Login that looks like your store. Themes cover the login, registration, password reset and email templates, so the moment a customer is most likely to abandon does not look like a different site.

How do you move customers without a password reset?​

A forced password reset at cutover costs you customers. A fraction will not open the email, and some of those were about to buy something. Lazy migration avoids it: Keycloak checks each customer's password against your old system the first time they sign in, then stores its own hash and never asks the old system again.

The user migration extension does this with two endpoints you add to your legacy system: a GET that returns the user's profile and a POST that answers whether a password is correct. The sequence that works:

  1. Stand up the realm and theme first, and point a staging copy of the storefront at it.
  2. Add the two legacy endpoints and configure the User migration using a REST client provider under User federation.
  3. Run old and new side by side. Customers who sign in through Keycloak are migrated on that login; everyone else is still served by the old system until you switch them.
  4. Move the web storefront, then back-office tools.
  5. Move the mobile app last. App releases go through store review and customers update on their own schedule, so the old login has to keep working for older app versions until they age out.
  6. Bulk-import the long tail who never signed in during the window, and send those customers a reset email when they return.

One thing to know before you do this: while migration is running, a sign-in for an email address Keycloak has not seen yet is checked against your legacy endpoint. Credential stuffing aimed at the new login therefore lands on the old system too. Rate-limit and monitor those endpoints like the public login they effectively are.

If you are coming from a hosted provider rather than your own database, the Auth0 to Keycloak walkthrough covers the export and the password-hash problem in detail.

What do attackers try against a store's Keycloak?​

These are patterns we have seen against production realms we run and support. None of them needs a vulnerability in Keycloak; each uses a default or a gap in the configuration.

  • They try every way in, not just your login page. A realm ships with built-in clients, and the admin CLI client accepts a password posted straight to the token endpoint. That path renders no page, so a CAPTCHA on your login page never sees it. Block one entry point and the traffic moves to the next one within hours.
  • A CAPTCHA that fails open is not a CAPTCHA. A login step that records a failed challenge and then lets the attempt continue looks fine in the admin console and stops nothing. Test it by posting a login without a token and checking you are refused.
  • Lockout does not stop credential stuffing. Brute force detection counts failures per user. A stuffing run tries one leaked password per email address and moves on, from a different residential IP every few attempts, so no single account or address ever crosses a threshold.
  • Your own services become the casualty. If a backend service signs in with a shared admin username and password, an attacker hammering that username locks the account, and your order sync goes down with it. Services should use client credentials, which have no password to guess.
  • Successful logins are the hard part to find. Failed attempts are loud. The accounts that matter are the ones where the leaked password worked, and those only show up in the event store, which by default keeps events for a short window.

The admin-cli and account client post covers which built-in clients to leave on at go-live and why, and Credential Stuffing and Account Takeover is the full prevent, detect and respond guide.

How does Phase Two layer the defenses?​

No single control stops credential stuffing, so we stack them. On a Phase Two dedicated cluster:

LayerWhat it doesWhere it is configured
Edge rate limitsPer-IP request limits at the edge, sized to your cluster tier, with a 429 and Retry-After when a source exceeds themSet by us; see Rate Limiting
CAPTCHA on login and registrationCloudflare Turnstile authenticators are included in every cluster image; you add your Cloudflare site key and place them in your flows so a failed challenge blocks the loginYou turn it on; see Turnstile
Admin path restrictionsLimits the Admin Console and Admin API to your office or VPN addresses (Premium and Enterprise)Dashboard; see Cluster Restrictions
No exposed master realmThe master realm is not customer-accessible, so there is no cluster-wide admin login to attackManaged by us
Events, metrics and logsLogin events are captured automatically; login volume, failure rates and logs are available to your on-call teamAudit Logs, Metrics, Logs
Go-live hardeningPassword grant off with client policies, unused self-service clients disabled, brute force detection onYou apply it; our go-live checklist lists every item

Two of these are worth being plain about. Turnstile is ready in every cluster but is not switched on until you configure it, because it needs your own Cloudflare account and a flow change only you can approve. And per-IP rate limiting on its own does not stop a distributed stuffing run; it stops a single source from overwhelming the cluster. The CAPTCHA, the closed password grant and the event monitoring are what deal with the distributed case.

What else should a store plan for?​

Peak season. Size the cluster for the busiest hour of the year, not the average. Our tiers are sized by active users (see Dedicated Clusters), and per-IP limits apply to your own traffic too: a backend that calls Keycloak for every order from one address, or a store full of customers behind one carrier NAT, can hit a limit a home shopper never will. Tell us before a launch or a load test so we can size it and tell it apart from an attack.

Long-lived mobile sessions. Customers expect the app to stay signed in for weeks. That usually means offline tokens and refresh token rotation, and rotation has a trap: two parts of the app refreshing at the same moment can sign the customer out. The fix belongs in the app, with one refresh in flight at a time. The invalid_grant post shows the failure and the settings involved.

Guest checkout. Do not make sign-in a condition of buying. Guest checkout stays in your store, not in Keycloak; offer account creation after the order is placed, when the customer has a reason to want one, and attach the order to the new account.

Remediation before you need it. Decide now what you will do when a stuffing run gets through: how you find the accounts where the password worked, how you reset them, and how you revoke their sessions, including the offline sessions a mobile app holds, which an ordinary logout leaves in place.

When should a store not do this?​

If your platform already provides customer accounts you are happy with (a hosted commerce platform's built-in login, for example) and you have one storefront and no app, adding Keycloak is a second system to run for little gain. It earns its place when you have more than one surface to sign into, B2B customers, a mobile app, or a homegrown login you no longer want to own.

Do this next​

Before you migrate anyone, stand up a realm, turn off the password grant, add a CAPTCHA to the browser flow, and try to sign in to it the way an attacker would: post a password to the token endpoint, then post the login form without a CAPTCHA token. If either works, you have found your first go-live item.
